THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Woody Herman by Herb Wong
Cassette 1

Washington, D. C.
December 28, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5895
PROCEEDINGS

MR. WONG: This is a special interview with Woody Herman, and I'm Herb Wong, the interviewer. It is part of the Jazz Oral History Project, sponsored through the funds of the National Endowment of the Arts and conducted by the Smithsonian Institution.

The interview was conducted in two segments, the first in Hollywood, in Woody's residence in December of 1978, and the second part in Berkeley, a few weeks later, in January. The interview consumed approximately six hours of time. And here's how it went.
MR. WONG: -- with Woody Herman at his residence in Hollywood. December 20, 1978. Woody, You just returned from New York, right?
Yes.
You just finished playing back East in a tour?

Well, actually we were in Florida about ten days ago, and we went down there for three dates and worked the Carolinas coming back, and got into Virginia and then finally into New York for a couple of private Christmas parties.
Okay.
(Recording interrupted.)
Well, I'd like to talk to you about your early dates first, so we can do this on a somewhat chronological, developmental order for the archives of the Smithsonian Institute.
Could you discuss how you got started, how did it really begin for you? That is, your motivations and early training?

Well, it's very difficult, really, because I've lived a long time, I can't remember the earliest things, but I still recollect the fact that my father and mother were very interested in my having some sort of musical career, preferably in the theatre.

And with this in mind, my father, who I guess was a frustrated singer, to some degree, decided I would be the completion of his ambitions. And so he taught me to sing and later I studied a little bit of dancing. But his whole intent was to make me a performer of one kind of another, and I guess he must have been able to do that, because I did my first tour when I was nine years old. And with some of the money I earned from that tour, which was a summertime tour, I was able to buy a saxophone and then later, a clarinet.
What were you doing on that tour?
Singing and dancing.
Singing and dancing.
And it was a kid unit.
Oh, it was?

Yeah, a unit of young children. And we were doing a prologue to a movie. And the movie was a Booth Tarkington story, called "School Days," which -- I guess he had made his reputation with "Penrod" and "Penrod and Simon" and those things for a movie for a child. A young man starred in the silent motion pictures by the name of Wesley Barry. [Berry]
And actually, what I was supposedly doing was playing the part of -- in the prologue, of Wesley Barry. And -- who was a frecklefaced kid, and I don't know where these thoughts came from --
(Recording interrupted.)
-- that I had to sing and dance, along with other kids.
I see.

And after I got the saxophone and clarinet, which was the same year, I started to study with local Milwaukee teachers, and fortunately for me I came across some very -- or, it was suggested to my parents, some very good people.

And so I learned my basic fundamentals from that. But earlier I had started with a few piano lessons, and I even at one point had a violin. So from the time I could actually walk and talk, I had some kind of musical instruments available to me, and someone usually prodding me to practice it and get into it.

And consequently, I then incorporated the music into my song and dance bit, the instrumental versions. And did that until about the time of my entrance, -- my freshman year in high school. I was now to the point, as I remember, of being completely bored and not finding this amusing anymore. It was fun in the very early stages. I suppose any kid likes attention, and it did give me lots of attention. But as I started to grow up and mature, I decided I really didn't like all that, and I wanted to have more time to play with other kids.
And then, when I got into high school, my freshman year, I became truly interested in -- via some early jazz records, and became involved that way.
Do you recall what some of those --

Yeah, some of the earliest things that were influencing me at the time were pieces played by such groups as the Indiana Five, Red Nichols, because I liked all the soloists that he was able to have on his records, and then I also -- one of the earliest records I had was Duke Ellington, when he had an eight-piece group known as the Washingtonians. And it sounded to me like jungle music. And I guess at some point it was even called a jungle band.
Yes.
And I found this to be very exciting and very different from anything I had ever heard or felt, and so consequently I -- all these things made a big influence.
When were you born, now?
May 16, 1913, in Milwaukee.
And you mentioned records. Were there records in your home, your family home?

Some, but not a great deal. Actually, the earliest records I bought on my own and got some sort of phonograph. But radio was just coming in very strong, and that was influencing all of us. And so I had, I guess, one of the early Atwater Kents in my room, and I was able to listen to music and bands particularly, and stay awake all night. It was very nice.
That's very nice. Was there any connection to any formal or academic music education in your school?

No, not the school I attended. Where I spent most of my years was at St. John's Cathedral Grade School and then later high school, and there was not -- they had a semblance of a band program, but not very much. But I was called upon to play constantly while I was a member of that grouping in school.
I see.
And I kept studying with private teachers, people like Arthur Buech.
Who?
Buech.
How do you spell that?

B-u-e-c-h. And another man by the name of Arthur Kruger. And they were both very fine. And actually, later I took some lessons from a man by the name of [Veesee] Walker, whose son was here in California and has been for a number of years, I believe, and he was music director and head of the band program at USC for a number of years, Tom Walker.

And at one point, I guess maybe when I was about 12, 13, I managed to get a couple of very instructive periods with Rudy Weedoff when he was touring and happened to be in Milwaukee. And it was arranged for me to have a couple of hours with him. And I think he taught me a great deal.
I see. That's very interesting. Was there kind of a continued support from your father, about what you were getting into now?
Well, actually, the support was beginning to run thin at the point when I had definitely made up my mind I was going to be a musician and not a performer.
I see.
And then, my father and my mother both didn't think that this was too good. They didn't feel it was favorable as far as my future was concerned.
And it was -- oh, they never really got strong about it with me, fortunately, and we didn't lose any love for each other in any sense of the word. But they were not as enthu-

siastic about my future as a musician as they might have been if I had remained a performer. Consequently, the big change came, of course, when I started to become a bandleader and have a band of my own, where I stood in front of the band. And then, of course, their attitudes changed completely.
Were they very familiar with -- or, how familiar were they with the music at that time? Were they interested in that?

No, I think, though, that my father and my mother, but my father particularly, had pretty good judgment and a natural sense of taste about what was good and what was bad. And that was my earliest guidance, and he was always interested and he was always willing to listen to something new and different. He wasn't the kind of human being that just decides they have a certain period in their lives when they listen, and then they turn it off.
I see. Were there instruments in the household?

Constantly. We had pianos and anything that could produce some kind of music. And my father was one of the early owners of an electric grand piano that played piano rolls. And he had all the semi-classics and classical pieces, and done by very fine artists, so it was -- that was a big influence. I heard a lot of music I would not have heard.
All right, let's see. Oh, yeah. Did you
really consider this as a career-oriented thing when you were playing in the, say, high school period? Were you looking toward it as a --

Yeah, I'm afraid I must have been, because, for instance, somehow or other, through friends and people I worked with in the theatre and so on, I was able to gather a number of brochures which were put out as advertising pieces, I guess, by Music Corporation of America and other agencies, but mainly the MCA ones, I remember, because they had marvelous photographs of all these bands they handled, in full regalia and uniforms and thousands of instruments in front of each player.

And this was very, very impressive to me, and as a matter of fact, I think right then and there, that at whatever age I was, -- and it had to be still in grade school -- that was what I wanted to do. That was bigger than being a ball player or anything else.
(Recording interrupted.)
All right. Some of the people you were interested in as players at the time.
Well, from those early records, particularly with the Red Nichols sides, I got to hear people like Benny Goodman for the first time.
Oh.
And even earlier sessions, I heard

people -- oh, what's the clarinetist? Earlier than Peewee Russell and people like that. This was a Chicago clarinetist and he played very well, and he impressed me. I just can't think of the name for the moment.
Marty Marsala?
No, it's way before that.
Before that?

MR. HERMAN: But I think also the fact that I was hearing these growling sounds from the Ellington group and uses of plungers with the trumpets and trombones and -- this all impressed me very much, along with the early Barney Bigard. And I wasn't -- and Frank Trumbauer was naturally a big influence. I think he had to be a big influence on some other people, because he was the first one to use the glissando as a means of making his feelings known, and I think Johnny Hodges would have to feel pretty much the same way as I did.

I first heard -- and it's an amazing thing, but when you're very young, a difference in age of a matter of four or five years is a big difference. And as you grow older, it becomes less and less important. But I do remember hearing Jack Teagarden for the first time. It was on one of the Red Nichols records. And I never could get -- I never could get over the fact that I -- it just gave me the feeling that this man had never made a mistake in his whole life, and didn't plan on making any, musically speaking.

And this gives a person -- I realized then what a great feeling of relaxation and assurance it gives your audience, if you're that kind of player. Because not so many were. And I felt a great deal of admiration and respect for him. For that reason, and many others, of course.

But these were some of the earliest sounds that I do remember, and just as I thought he was so fantastic, I was not impressed, for instance, by Miff Mole. I couldn't find anything happening. And yet, he was very fluent and a very together trombone player for those times and days. And, of course, to me Benny Goodman as time went on proved that he was a genius at keeping the instrumental sound of an instrument where it should be and being able to convey his thoughts and ideas as he did.
Did any of these groups come by your home town, early on?

Later, but by that time I was in high school and I was now in the house band at the Eagles Ballroom. And we had many bands coming in across the country to play opposite, including Paul Whiteman. So I got to meet a lot of these people whom I had been hearing only on records and on the radio, and getting to meet them. And these were important times for me, very important.
This house band, was it something that was weekly, or every --
No, it was five nights a week and we had one matinee.
Is that right? What kind of shows?

Well, it was a ballroom. It was for dancing and they had two big bands, the house band and a travelling band in constantly. And all the hit bands, people like Coon- Saunders and Austin Wiley would come in from Cleveland. So I got to hear a lot of players that I ordinarily would not have heard.
Yeah, that's marvelous.
It was a great kind of ground to lay the groundwork with.
What was the makeup of this house band instrumentally?

As I remember, we had about four brass, three or four. I think, two trumpets, two trombones, sometimes maybe three trumpets if you were lucky. And maybe three saxophones, two altos and a tenor. And if there were four, sometimes a baritone.
And you were playing saxophone and clarinet?
I was playing tenor and clarinet at that point.
I see. Did you do any singing that early?
Oh, yeah, yeah. Because I sang -- that
came from vaudeville.
Vaudeville, I see. Was there a leader that you recall, of this band?

Oh, yeah, his name was Joe Lichter. He was a man originally from Milwaukee, who had been a theatre conductor and a theatre musician most of his life. He'd done a lot of work in Chicago and he came back to Milwaukee. And he had the orchestra conductor at the Strand Theatre there for several years, and then when the theatres were getting a bit shaky, he switched to going to a ballroom, because he was basically a kind of a jazz player himself.
Well, that's good.
So it made it very much better for young people like myself to find a niche.
Did you learn anything about the kind of leadership functions from this man?

Oh, maybe, but -- and I was very -- I was so very much interested, as were most young musicians in being aware of everything that was happening around me and everything that was going down. And consequently, I think every one I ever worked for was some kind of influence on me. Maybe some influenced me to the point where I never wanted to be like they were, but that's the chance you take.
How did you get on this house band? Did they hear about you playing at school, or --

No, I think it was through some of the musicians in the band who were aware of me and knew I could do several things, and when the leader was looking for someone, they suggested (unintelligible) to him. Because I had some major weaknesses, like, my reading was very poor. Because I was never really in a position to read. I would practice and play the exercises and the chords and scales, and I would play and I would perform them.

So I had never really gotten around to a thing of having to read. And it was kind of a challenge the first few months, but the older people in the band, particularly the saxophone players, were kind enough to work with me and help me, right.
This kind of rubbed off through your career, a lot. Them helping you and you helping --

Well, I think that's prevalent in all of jazz music, particularly any music where you're supposedly creating something. One player will certainly help another, in 99 percent of the cases. And I think that feeling of camaraderie is a great thing.
How long were you on this house band?
Until the time I left Milwaukee, which would be my senior year in high school.
I see.
And I joined another band and went to
Chicago, to join them, naturally. It was Tom Garen's band, a San Francisco band. And that was my first time in San Francisco.
(Recording interrupted.)

Tom Garen was a very important influence on me, because I think he taught me a very great deal about music as a business. Tom was a businessman, and he was not in any sense of the word a musician you would look up to as an incentive to want to play better or something. But he did have a good sense of logic and he had a feeling for what the public would like. And the truth of the matter is that I would say that the majority of the bands during the late -- early '30s, actually, and even later, were really built on a pattern to find favor with an audience, and the quality of music really was secondary.

It was entirely up to the person's own judgment as to whether -- how important music was going to be in his particular band. And I learned a great deal from Tom, not because it was the best musical band I worked in, but because it was a great entertainment band. He had some very important people in the band, like Ginny Simms, a girl singer who later went to Kay Kyser's band. And we had another young man in the saxophone section, along with myself. His name was Tony Martin. It was then Al Morris, and later in the motion picture world he became known as Tony Martin.
And we all -- and there were two or three other

singers in the band who sang very well. And consequently, it was an entertaining unit, and that was the basis for the band, with some reasonably good music being played because we had a good arranger and a good musical director by the name of Gary Nottingham.
He wound up with the band here in San Francisco.

Yes, and I stayed with Tom for about -- oh, I guess two and a half years. And when I did leave him it was supposedly to start my own group. And I ran into so many roadblocks that I wound up joining another band because I couldn't stand the waiting around for something to happen. And so I joined Harry Sosnick's band, which was a radio band, and doing one of its earliest and first and only tours, I think. And that band, we had some very fine musicians, mostly from the Chicago area. And I think it was a good transition move for me. But I finally got -- the best place to be for someone like myself at that point was to be with a band which was really musical and only concerned with music.

And I was growing a little bored with doing my show biz, once again. So I got this offer to go with Isham Jones, and the reason I got the offer was because about four or five guys in the band were friends of mine and knew what I could do musically, and got me the job with Isham.
But even someone who was a great songwriter and a

very good arranger, and a very good all-around musician, someone like Isham Jones, who certainly had a very good musical background, hired me, I think, mainly because he heard I could sing, dance, if necessary, and do many things, and because he knew a lot of saxophone players. It was as basic as that.
I see.

And -- however, it gave me a chance to prove what I wanted to do somewhat musically, and with -- my first actual recording dates were with the Isham Jones band. I did some earlier with Tom Garen's band, but they were once again entertainment quality records. And this was my first -- little more musical experience, and eventually we had -- our first jazz date was done as a small group, and we were the Isham Jones Juniors. And it was really my group, along with the rhythm section and maybe a trumpet, and Joe Bishop on flugelhorn or something.
I see.

So it was a good experience for me, and as a matter of fact, we all by that point -- I did especially, had my own desires as to where -- what kind of music to play. And I was certainly interested in the jazz of that time. And the Ben Pollack band was a great favorite of mine, along with Benny's band and everyone else who was into playing swinging music.
And so, when Isham decided to retire in 1936, early

in '36, that's when we had a couple of meetings, the guys in the Isham Jones band and myself. And about five of us eventually stuck together, with the intent of doing what the Bob Crosby band had done, which originally had been the Pollock band, and that was to set up a corporation, and each member, at least of the original grouping, would be stockholders. And then we would hire the musicians and work as a going unit. And so that's how the first band started, and I was more or less -- there was never any serious discussion about who would stand in front of the band or anything, because I guess I was expected to, and that's the way it turned out.

And for the first few years, we operated as a -- quite a few years, about eight or nine years, we operated as a cooperative band. The only problem with that, I found, as the guy who stands in front of it, you have to have board meetings if you want to go to the men's room, and this gets to be a pretty heavy thing.
So I decided then that if there was ever going to be a change, it would be to just have one leader and one person to operate the thing. How the money would get distributed was something else.
So that was dissolved?
It was dissolved, because eventually, during the way, almost everyone who was originally with me was drafted out, or they left of their own accord, because the
going was very rough, and so then I wound up with the thing.
I see. That's a good recap on that. Were you playing alto then, already? Because you mentioned tenor.

No, I didn't. I was playing tenor with Isham, and sometimes baritone, and I was doing mostly clarinet soloing. And then when we started the band, I was going to play clarinet exclusively, and not mess with the saxophone section at all. And I did, for several years. I had a temperamental alto player, it doesn't matter who it was, who gave us a lot of problems, and particularly on one record date or another. And I became a little annoyed and borrowed an alto from one of the other guys, and played a couple of things with the section, and also a solo or something.

And we decided that maybe that would be the best move. And I played some of those things. And in the interim, I had Johnny Hodges come in and do a couple of our record dates, and Ben Webster and a lot of other people, because Ellington's band was -- it was one of those periods with Duke's band where the boys were getting nervous in the band. They were complaining that Duke was taking their backgrounds and making tunes out of them, and a lot of internal strife for that moment. And so they were all -- I would hear from them if I didn't call them about doing some record dates with us. And so we would add them to the band.
How was that relationship between you and
first connected-- members of the Ellington organization, Johnny and Ben and --

Well, it was just because they knew what we were into, and they felt the band was trying something. And whether they agreed that what we were doing was the greatest or not, but they also knew that there was some bread to be gotten, plus the fact that they wouldn't be asked to do something that was foreign to their nature musically. So I think it worked out very well. As a matter of fact, the very first person out of Duke's band that came with us had already left the band, and that was Juan Tizol. And he was the first big complainer about what was happening with the tunes, and there was some kind of strife going on there. So consequently, as I say, if I didn't call them, they would call us and want to know if there were any record dates coming up. And I think that was one of the periods, too, when the band was struggling a bit, in the early '40s.
In the early '40s.
Yeah. In fact, everybody was.
You continued the contract with Decca Records then that Isham had had when he left.

Well, it was a new contract and a whole new thing -- yeah, same company, however, yeah. No, we actually played for the people at Decca, the Kapp Brothers, and then we became almost like a house band there the first couple or three years. That was about the only thing that kept us
together, because work was very -- well, we had a job right from the beginning, Roseland, which didn't pay very well. But we managed to stay there for a lot of months.

And then, when we went out to go on the road because we'd had some air time, along with a few records released, we couldn't be booked very well. And so consequently, for a year or two it was a real battle to stay alive, to make it work. And if we hadn't had Decca going, we probably would have collapsed completely. But eventually we got a couple of records that got some play and eventually went back to New York, after hanging out in New England along with a lot of other bands, trying to eke out an existence.
Went back to New York and opened a place called The Famous Door on 52nd Street, and then things started to perk up a little.
Well, you did numerous records, a whole long string, for --
Well, we were almost like a house band at that -- yeah.
As I recall, even in some of the tunes, reflected the policy of that day, that everyone was trying to cover a tune.
Yeah, that's right. If there was a hit on Victor, then Decca -- we'd be in to do it the next week.
You had a lot of vocals.
Yeah, yeah.
And you had a small group, too.

Well, they allowed us to do that so we could get involved in the jazz thing, which we were all interested in. And they knew that that's what I wanted to do, so they allowed me to do that. But that took a while, that didn't happen right from the beginning.
I see.
In other words, do two for them and I might get to do one later.
Uh-huh. Were you -- you had a good group of competent people in your band.
Oh, yes, and we were constantly trying to improve it, and getting better writing and better everything.
Who were some of the people who contributed significantly to that period?

Well, the early period, of course, would have to include people like Frankie Carlson, a drummer who did a good job for us, Tommy Linehan, a pianist, Walt Yoder, the bassist. Everyone was important in that first band, as far as what they were producing. Joe Bishop, of course, did a masterful job of writing tunes for the band, writing arrangements for the band, and then switching over from tuba, which he played with Isham, to flugelhorn with our band.
And then, we had a lot of outside contributors,

well, people who were really not outside, because Cordon Jenkins, for instance, who had been arranging for the Jones band when we were with him contributed because he knew we didn't have any bread, wrote some things for us, and this helped us. And a lot of good writers -- and James Noble wrote for the band for quite a while, and later, Nick Harper -- Harper is his original name -- a fiddle player. He wrote a lot of music for the band, and a lot of it was very different. He wrote a swinging arrangement of Meditation from Pais. And he wrote the melody line, and the band was shouting in back of him and you could never find him. And he loved it.
Were you in some way pulling things together from the variety of contributors to fit the direction that you had? Did you edit things then?

Well, yeah, to some degree I think I did. I'm pretty sure I did, because -- and when I didn't, I was being shoved and pushed around by the powers that be at Decca, because they really knew what they wanted, and I learned a great deal from their operation, Jack and particularly Dave Kapp. Because Dave was the guy that used to take the truck out, the sound truck, and go into the South and try to discover folk and blues and people, and do it right on the spot. And he had a goodly supply and an unlimited kind of repertoire to offer things for me to record.
I see.
Which led to such things as "Troubling Mind, Dupree Blues," and so on and so on and so on. And he made me more and more aware of a certain kind of American folk and blues kind of thing.
So he was --
He was a big influence in his day.
-- that -- I think it was eight or ten 78's, records in the Blues on Parade album. That was kind of a --

And he gave me a pretty free hand on any of those things. Once he got the idea to make -- but by the same token, he would turn around and in the same week that he gave me two or three of these things, would turn around and call me in and say, this record is breaking very big over on RCA Victor, but I've got a lyric written for you and I want you to sing. I'll give you the title in just a second. (Singing.)
"Frenesi."
Frennessee, right. So where Hardy had a big record on this instrumentally, we did very well. We sold a lot of records with my singing way up in the air with a lot of muted trumpets in the background.
I see.
So they were very helpful in a lot of ways, and it was always -- they knew what they were seeking, and I was still finding where I wanted to go. So a lot of
times, I think I did, and so did the guys in the band, feel we were being maneuvered. But it was probably best for us in the long run.
At that time, yeah.
Yeah.
Were there any unusually large sales records for any particular record that you had? 'The Wood-chopper's Ball' (inaudible).

Well, that was pretty good, but it was constant -- Decca had another good system, which would be wonderful if somebody picked up on it today. If they thought a thing had something but never really got off to a flying start, they wouldn't just discard it, every once in a while they would try it again. And that's what happened with 'Wood-chopper's Ball,' because it must have been out three different times. And over a period of time, several years, it became a giant.

But I don't think that's done anymore. I don't think they have the patience to wait, to see if something could happen. But whatever, I did feel that I learned a lot there, and I certainly was able to apply some of it later. Before I left Decca, it was a transition period, and some of those things are still available, where you can -- when Chubby and Dave Tough and all those people were around, in the band, and we were trying -- as a matter of fact, some of Ralph Burns'

first arrangements for our band were done on Decca. But -- and I really wasn't as -- I didn't think it was so terribly important. My contract was finally coming to a close, but I didn't think it was all that important to leave Decca, except for one thing: The sound of the Decca studios used to drive me crazy. It never had the same kind of thing that Columbia and Victor had.
I see.

Whether it was a question of engineering or what, I don't know. But I do know it was inferior to my ears. And so what I did before I made up my mind where we were going to go, because we had offers from both the other labels, was to do V-discs in Columbia, in the church downtown. And also at the RCA main studios, and then I decided I liked the Columbia sound the best and that's why we wound up going to Columbia. For no other reason.
Is that so?
I wonder how many people would do that today?
I don't think it would happen in circumstances today. That's right, you did a number of things in World War II V-discs. I see them even reappearing today on -- as collectors' items reissues.
Bootlegger items.
I saw some in Sacramento about two or three weeks ago. You were beaming your music overseas, too,
that way.
Yes, uh-huh.
Were you on radio yet?
Oh, yeah. We were on radio right from the start, right at Roseland, when Mutual was a chain.
Oh, yeah.

Those early days. But it really didn't take on any great effect for us or great coverage until the band became somewhat important via records, and then all of a sudden we started to get much better airtime and a lot more -- that's when we started playing major hotels in New York or wherever it was and if we had to lose $2,000 or $3,000 a week, it didn't matter because we were getting the right kind of airtime.
And then, when we left that engagement and went on the road, the money would come back. That was the way it was done in those days, with all the bands.
Because there were over 100 or more bands.
Right.
There was tremendous competition for this radio time.
Yes, right, exactly.
Today it's a different kind of competition and different kinds of groups, but it's still competition.
Yeah, exactly, sure.
You were one of the first -- if not most of it -- people who had started to use female instrumentalists. You had Billie Rogers on trumpet.

Yeah, she was first with the band. That would be about '41, I think. And then later, in '44, I hired Hyams, Marjorie Hines, a very good vibra-harpist. As a matter of fact, she was there and then she was followed by Red Norvo, so she wound up in very good class. And when she left the band, she went with George Shearing's first sextet.
What was your feeling about incorporating the vibes and other instruments? You've had different instruments, because you had the guitar --

Well, I was constantly seeking other colors, you know, as to what it could be and still be able to get a good swinging thing going. And that's why in those years I guess we were starting to use the sound of vibes, clarinet, guitar and piano. And Ralph had the great ability of writing for these odd instrumentations and -- odd at the time -- and making it happen, especially against the big band.
How did he get on the band? Did you recruit him?

No, as a matter of fact, there was a whole contingent -- well, not that many, a couple-three came directly from the Charlie Barnet band. I didn't know that they had been with Charlie until much later. But Ralph was with
Charlie's band and so was Chubby, and so was Francis Lane. Wayne.

And -- but I think they felt that they would be able to express themselves a little more fully, coming with us, and that's what happened. That was a transition period, and that's when we -- then I started to look for people and found people like Bill Harris and -- who'd been in a few bands, but no one had really utilized him. And from there, -- as a matter of fact, he had just done the Benny Goodman -- the a picture with Benny Goodman, prior to joining me. And I think that was probably the first time he was really -- where he had a chance to play anything.

And then Flip Phillips came in the band. I got him from Russ Wes Morgan's band in New York. And he stayed with the band about a month, and then he got worried because he figured that Russ Wes Morgan was a much more working band, and that his success -- and he would be able to call his shots and be able to keep everybody happy, working.

So he left the band, and then about a month later, we were starting to get some -- we were around the Paramount Theatre for ten weeks at a crack or something, and all of a sudden, Flip was ready to rejoin. But he was always very skeptical, and I think that proved it.
Oh, I see. Well, that's historically one of the most heavily important bands.
Well, it was an exciting and different

kind of band for the time. I remember hearing -- I still hear from guys and people in general, particularly if they had been away, had been overseas, about hearing the first record that came from Columbia, or the second one or the third one, that said, I just didn't believe their music could change so. ""

Actually, we hadn't changed so, as far as I could see. But it was a new excitement, I guess, and when they came back to the States, they were just -- they flip out if we play that at our in-person engagements.
Of course, the band was reflecting the evolution of the music, too. You had some bop-oriented things that were going on in music.
Right.
Kind of a bridge between the Duke-ish, Louis-ish period.

That's right. My earliest influences came back and Ralph was very heavily influenced by Sweetpea and by Duke and so we were all shooting for the same thing. We didn't want to be like Duke, but we sure wanted to sound good like him.

In other words, Charlie took the other thing, -- Barnet -- and did an actual copy of Duke's music, and that to me would have been very distasteful, and that would be dishonoring a great man and a great group of musicians. But what we did was try to capture the feeling, warmth and enthu-
siasm, and if we could outswing him, then we'd figure we'd won the game.
And at that time, most of the fellows in your band, they were pretty young guys.
Oh, yeah. They were comparable to any band I've ever had in age.
Yeah, that's right. Upstart band.
Yeah, sure. Young blood and all that came out of there.
Was there a particular attitude by Columbia that started to happen with the kind of music that you were quite successful with?
They gave us a very free hand.
They did?

Very. And, of course, I was there during a period which was not a long one, where a guy -- Manny Sachs, who was Sinatra's man, and he liked music and he had a flare for putting good things together. And very few suggestions, other than, 'Can I do something for you?'
Really.
That's right.
What was the mode of promotions at that time, as you look back?
Well, the mode of promotion in our case was the only smart business arrangement I ever did in my life,

probably. And I don't think you can call it a business arrangement, but I'm pretty sure that there were a lot of my contemporaries, particularly those on Columbia, who never knew at the time what was happening.

My idea with Columbia Records was not how much money or how many pressings or any of the things that I knew were pretty difficult in the wartime, because there were too many limitations in the situation. So what I did ask Mr. Sachs for was the same amount of exploitation, publicity and press, -- whatever you want to call it, advertising, that their top two stars, their top two people -- and their top two people were, to the best of my recollection, Frank Sinatra and Dinah Shore.
I see.

And every time there was an ad in Variety or Billboard or any other kind of exploitation, I had it. And I'm sure that Les Brown, Harry James, and everybody else there was wondering, many times, 'What the hell is going on?'
Yeah, there were a lot of other bands on the same label, Charlie Spivak --
(End of Side One.)

I think that was probably the most thrilling -- it was, undoubtedly, that ever happened in my musical career and life. To receive a telegram from Igor Stravinsky, saying that he had heard some of our music and he

was now writing a piece -- he was writing a piece for the Woody Herman band. And this -- I received this, I think, probably along about October, this telegram. And he said, "I hope to have the piece completed and will come to New York and bring it in time for Christmas to you -- to the men in the band and you."

And, imagine having something like this happen to someone in my position or the guys, and, well, I flipped out and so did the guys in the band. It was all arranged through a mutual friend who actually became some way or other a music publisher, but not as a publisher but as a song plugger for a publisher. But he was a very astute guy, and he was a former bassist, he'd been in a couple of bands. And somehow, he got to latch on to Mr. Stravinsky and he started to play our records for Mr. Stravinsky. Then I believe that somewhere along the line he decided that he was going to write a piece for this group of mad young people.

And eventually, he did bring it to New York and it was presented to us, and we -- he rehearsed it and taught it to us, actually, because we weren't that accomplished, to play pure Stravinsky, because that's what it was. It wasn't jazz, nor was it meant to be. As he put it, the challenge was to write for with such bastard instrumentation, and he did add, -- he said, because he had to add a horn and a harp.
I see.

And -- but basically, it was his music, as it should have been. And we learned to play the music, and presented it at Carnegie Hall in 1946, at our first jazz concert. And the critique was quite broad, some of it with great gusto and enjoyment and some of it couldn't understand what it was about and so consequently I would say it would remind me of some of the things that still happen.

however, And, all in all, we took the thing on the road then and [played ] it every night, and did a concert tour. Then, when we got to the Coast, Mr. Stravinsky was now home, and he lived not far from here (inau- where we're sitting. dible). And we decided we would record it, and do an album or whatever you would call them in those days.
That was 12-inch, wasn't it?
I think so, yes, an album. And he said, "I would never cut my music, but," he said, "I will for you."
(Laughter.)

So this is why I feel that -- and then, of course, the man who was so great at Columbia Records, whom I didn't mention earlier because I was only concerned with really the pop department, the man, Goddard Lieberson, who was head of the serious department and so on, and a very artistic man and a man who really treated the whole music thing with dignity. I'm glad I had the good fortune to be associated with some of these people. John Hammond was there, who really wasn't into our band because we were a little too far out for him. But he
would still be enthusiastic about for everything we did. And if you've ever had the feeling of having a company behind (unintelligible), you, we did. That was very important in those days.
That's marvelous.
Just as -- I would say in comparison would be with Stan Kenton and the way Capital believed in him and worked and allowed him his head, with him (unintelligible).
Okay. Didn't you tell me some anecdotal things about how the band was playing flying somewhere, and they were rehearsing and they I'd have had to come back downstairs --
Oh, yeah, that was with Mr. Stravinsky. We rehearsed --he arrived while we were doing an engagement at the Paramount Theatre.
That's it.

And it was a long engagement, I think eight or ten weeks. And I don't know just when this transpired, except on his arrival, the whole band hurried after the first show to get to this rehearsal hall on the top floor, but everyone stopped in the dressing rooms to change clothes and put on a dark blue suit and shirt and tie and things that are not normal with musicians, because it was such a great honor that this man had come.
So Stravinsky arrived, wearing a sweatshirt and a pair of slacks and a towel around his neck. He was ready to go to work. And so we rehearsed for about an hour, an hour

and a half, as long well as we could. And then the buzzer buzzed, and he was really having a marvelous time, and telling me what a lovely family I had and how pleased he was that the music sounded as good as it did and so on.

And then he would go downstairs to -- someone would escort him downstairs to go to Sardi's, which was next door and have a little something, a little vodka and a little something there, a little champagne. Then they would say, 'Okav, we go back to rehearsal.' So he'd come back up, and we had just come out of the pit and did another show.

Well, this went on all day and all night. Finally, by the second day, someone got over the fact that -- no one wanted to really mention it -- the fact that we could only stay so long, we had to come back and so on, because we were doing shows. He said, 'Oh, you're doing shows? That's lovely.' So he came down and finally watched our stage show, this was the third day.
Oh, that's remarkable.
Yeah, it's pretty amusing, but we were slowly going under from lack of energy.

But those were exciting times, and just as there will always be exciting times for anyone who's in a position to be experimenting and doing new things, with new music and so on. That's the lifeblood of the whole thing.
Did you have very much communication at
the time or interest from some of the small group, revolutionary bebop groups were having? I know you had some other kinds of musicians coming in and out.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, well, Dizzy started to write for our band. He did a couple --
(Recording interrupted.)

And then, too, I think the fact that Charlie Parker had made such a big dent into the whole jazz scene, and that we were all very conscious of this, as he, I guess, was conscious of what we were into, because he used to come over and sit in with the band, very often. And that was the reason that there was a tape, finally, from Kansas City which was a put-together date by someone, as far as a place to play together.
How did that come about?

It was supposedly an afternoon hangout, get-together, in Kansas City for a group of people that liked Charlie and liked our band, so they thought it would be marvelous. So that's how it came about. We didn't know anyone was taping it, however.
I see. Was that just a single concert?
Yeah, that's right, just one afternoon concert.
Do you recall when that was? '46?
I think it was later, it was '47.
I see, yeah.
Yeah.
Do you know what's become of that tape? Did it ever appear?

Yes, yeah, sure. It's released on some label out of Europe or somewhere. I the other dav was in New York, and in our bin at Sam Goody's I had certainly far more -- I was outnumbered in releases that are bootleg products than I was by legitimate. But we were well represented in everything.
There were a number of players in your band at that time that reflected Dizzy's influence.
Oh, yeah, Shorty Rogers, Red Rodney. Neal Hefti
Neal Hefti was, too.
Neal Hefti was a big influence, too. And Candi Candoli. Well, everyone was affected by the modern sounds of that period.
Yeah. Well, there weren't too many big bands at that time --
That were involved, yeah.
-- that were involved. Charlie had a little -- Charlie Barnet had a little bit of it, but I think yours really was the forefront.
Yeah, I think so, and I think the Four
" Brothers sound had a great deal to do with that, too. The fact that along with coming up with some bebop tunes and all, we came up with a new sound for a band.
Prior to that, I was going to might as well talk to you a little bit about the rhythm section in that first herd.
Davey Tough. Davie Tufts.

Oh, Davie Tufts set the pattern there, I think. In fact, I'm sure he did. I remember when I hired Well, Davey Tough Davie, Chubby was still new in the band, and he said, "Is that the guy that used to be with Tommy Dorsey?" And I said, "Yeah." He said, "Do you think he'll fit the band?" I said, "Oh, yeah," I said, "Yeah, he'll fit the band."
Well, anyway, two days later, after Davey got there, Chubby had decided he invented Davey. Davey.
(Laughter.)

No, but it was really -- they didn't believe that one person so diminutive, who looked like he was about ready to cave in most days, and really would -- had absolutely no technique, and didn't want any. So -- and yet, could propel a band and just make everybody -- put everyone into a relaxed position.
How do you do that? What's your feeling about it? How was he able to do that?
Well, I think that he was just a dynamic time keeper, that there was never one ever quite like him, who took

great pride in his cymbals, the sound of each one, the heads on his drums. He was a very musical person without realizing it. He didn't read or any of that stuff, but he was a meticulous musician as far as his taste and ability.
And he kept you straight, he kept you musically straight, plus timewise you were at home, no matter where you were.
I see. So dependable.

That's right. And it taught a great deal to people, some of the younger players that -- I think it's that they were forced to take on a different discipline than they were used to. This made for a very tight, big band.
Had you been aiming to get him?
Not really, except I always knew that he played with the right guys and he knew just what to do.
I see.
And it was just one of those things. I said if we're going to have to get a drummer that will fit with what we're into, we'd better get somebody who's going to keep us together.
I see.
And that was really my basic thinking, because Davy had been through every Dixieland contingent and through every other kind of contingent. Name it, he'd been there.

And, of course, when he had to leave the band and the guys made the replacement, really, because I did not know Don Lamont at that point at all. He was the discovery of the band, and then I found another kind of drummer who had a lot of Davey's attributes but also had something else going -- technique and fly and the fact that he was into the new music, very much so. And consequently, when I started the Second Herd and he came back in the band, I gave him a free hand. I said, 'Look, Davy, the rhythm section will keep playing what they're supposedly -- should be doing. But I want you to feel free to throw frills and bombs and do whatever you want whenever you feel it.'
I see.
So he had his own little launching pad going.
Yeah, yeah. So he did express himself even --
That's right.
That's great.
Sure, and that's why I think we were able to come up with certain kinds of things.
Do you feel that through all these decades that your way of encouraging musicians has paid off in more cases than not?
Oh, I think, generally speaking, espe-

cially in the last 30 years. I feel that I can help a player if he wants to be helped. Of course, he has to have that kind of feeling, too. If he decides I don't know what I'm talking about, we're in trouble.

But most times, and I think that's the one thing that I'm most proud of, is the fact that we do have a communication, and I still do and I will continue to have as long as I'm alive. And I don't -- for instance, I never ask a young musician how old he is. That comes much later. But people say, 'How old is he?' I have no idea. I don't care, really. That's such a dumb qualification, how old are you. Not, how do you play or -- you know. I don't think it's important at all.
How about Chubby's role? Now, he went through quite a number of (Inaudible) more than a decade.

Oh, yeah. Well, mostly Chubby was a very strong and good -- a very strong influence, first of all, and in most cases, very good. I think, though, that somewhere along the line, his not continuing his musical -- let's put it bluntly, his musical education --
Yeah, growth.

-- that music got too complex and that's when he left the scene, really, for any great intent. I think he still is a guy that certainly can swing a band and can help to swing a band and has generally very good musical taste.
But there's always going to be certain things that

he's not going to be ready to do because he didn't study enough to be able to facilitate the whole thing. And that's unfortunate in his case, because if Ray Brown is still an important bassist, then Chubby certainly should be.
I see, sure.
Yeah, because--
Looking at a parallel.
That's right.
Well, he was one of the spark plugs for kind of the spirit in the band.
Oh, yes, definitely. And he would still be, if he were there. Or anywhere. Wherever he is, there's a spark plug.
And Ralph, of course, he played a dual role for you, mostly both as pianist...
Yeah, and arranger, of course. His arranging ability is beyond anyone's concept, as far as I am concerned. There's no one that ever really touched him.
You want to talk about him at length? It seems that he's a subject that would be --

Well, I think that he's my biggest success. That's The only way I can express it. In other words, of all the people that I've known through my bands, he has gone the farthest and then, too, if I had to put a second one, I'd have to put from the broadness of his approach and his accep-

tance worldwide would be Stan Getz. But I don't think there's a comparison at all, because one man is a completely different kind of person than the other, and I think that -- I feel very strongly that Ralph's music still has not been heard. I would give anything if I were in a position, and he were in a position to spend the time, to write new music for me. Because I think it would probably be the epitome of everything I've done in my whole life, and maybe his, too.
I think we were good for each other.

Yes. You mentioned some of these things during your 40th anniversary, that you were reflecting back because he was coming back for the guest shot and so forth. Some of the ways you worked together -- how did you -- did you just leave it to his control? How much control and leadership did you exercise as far as direction?
Well, we had a very strange arrangement. I don't think anyone else in the music business probably had it quite like this, because I never heard about it.

In the first place, I -- my only commitment as far as what we were to do, starting with the basic material, if I came in with a tune that I felt had some possibilities, I might suggest that it might be nice done slowly, or it might be nice done at a swinging tempo, and that was it. And I'll see you later.
And then, when he would bring in that arrangement,

or any other arrangement, he would say, "Woody, this sort of goes like this or like this, " and then he might play me a little bit of it. And then he said, "And anything you don't think makes it, take it out."

And he is the one that gave me the confidence to imagine that I was an editor, because he was his very personal attitude of -- and later he would say, "That was fine, I'm glad you took that out, " or something, words to that effect, which gave me great confidence. Maybe it was undeserved, but at least I felt I wasn't -- we certainly weren't battling each other.

And sometimes I would like some phrase or some little thing and I would ask him to repeat it several times. And he probably thought I was mad with that, too, but I also thought that maybe it gave the thing a certain charm or something. No, I think we were -- I've always felt that we never had to worry about each other's weaknesses or strengths, you know, like, we could say just anything that came into our heads and it would be fine.
Wonderful.
We don't have many of those associations in life.
That's a rare one. Have you chatted with him in the last couple of years about doing something?
No, not -- since the anniversary was of the last time, but of course, we always talk about -- sure, we'll

have to get together and we'll do the thing." And when I've asked him to write a new piece for us, he'll say -- usually he has a -- even before the fact that I know he has more commitments than he can handle, is the fact that he'll say, I can't write any jazz, I haven't written jazz in years." One of those -- but if I could or if I was in a position -- I know for a fact that he tried very strongly to get our band to do a film he did last year, of New York, New York."
Oh, he did?
And the producer, director, whoever the person was, said he didn't want anyone so -- how do you say it, from a period that's still going or something. I don't know, it really didn't matter.

But what Ralph did anyway was to write whatever sounds there were to sound like our band. It didn't matter whether we played it or someone else did. In other words, he knew what he wanted for the period of that picture.
Sure, sure.
And for what it portrayed, as jazz musicians in life or something.
You had -- Neal Hefti did some things that fitted in nicely, too.
Oh, yeah, but not very much.
Not much, huh?
No, Neal was not a very productive
writer during that period of his life. He was too busy playing, still.
Yes, yeah.

And actually, he came up with a lot of ideas and a lot of head things that he put together or helped to put together, where everyone contributed. And some of the best things that were done in any of those pieces were Neal's. But actually, his full arrangements, I think, after The Good Earth and -- I'll name them all -- The Good Earth, Black Orchid and Let It Snow, Let It Snow, and one other, I can't think of what it is, were the only complete things that he brought in.
I see.
And the rest of the time, he was always in there, fixing something, changing it, and making some remarkable things happen.
That was his style, in a sense.
Yeah, yeah.
You seemed to have trumpet player writers. Shorty did some things.
Oh, yeah, he did a lot of good things for us, yeah.
You had some black musicians in your group -- Ernie Royal, Gene Ammons.
Yeah, Gene Ammons.
Milt Jackson, for a short time.
Yeah, Milt was with me quite a long time, and Oscar Pettiford. And then later I had a lot of -- who would come through the band for short periods, yeah.
Was this during times when World War II, mainly, people were going in and out of the service and --
Right, there was a lot of movement, a lot of movement, yeah. I had one very fantastic experience that I think should be related.

I had a band -- at this point, it was near the end of the Second Herd. And Shadow Wilson was on drums, and Oscar was still there, I believe -- I can't be positive about that. But Gene was and Ernie, and somebody else, I think.
Not Milt, Milt wasn't there.
No, it was right before Milt.
Before Milt.
And we were to begin a theatre tour of eight weeks or ten weeks, which we needed. You need the dates because of the financial overhead.

And I got a notice from the Loews Booking Corporation with a tour of their theatres, and we were starting at their flagship house in Washington, D. C. at the Loew's Capital Theatre. I got a very heavy note from the management of that theatre and one of the big stockholders of the Loew's Corporation, that I would appear with an all-white orchestra in his
theatre or I would not appear there or the rest of the Lowe's Theatre tour.

There was no question of talking it over or listening to anybody's presentation, nothing. This was a statement of fact. So I didn't know what to do. I discussed it with my lawyers and -- before the tour. So I called the black guys to the dressing room, and I said, "Look, if we're going to finish this tour, which I certainly -- I know we have to, if we're going to continue," I said, "What I will do just so I can get over this thing about getting into the papers and everything else, without" "I said, "I will pay all your salaries plus expenses to go back to New York and have a ball for a week." We go to Indianapolis or (inaudible) whatever it is, right?

So the poor guys -- somebody talked to his wife or whoever. By the time they arrived and got off the train back in New York, there was a battery of lawyers from the NAACP and the whole thing. And they kept them up all night, grilling them, trying to do something for their people and the whole thing. P.S.: They were back the following morning. And it was pretty ridiculous kind of situation. And they said they didn't know why they were back, but were told it's (unintelligible) "Well, look, fellows, I'm not going to argue, you can do whatever you like, because it's bigger than I am. But I will tell you this: If you insist on staying here and going back to work, I'm certainly not going to prevent you. But I'll
tell you one thing, tomorrow morning I'll be back on my hill in California, and that's the end of me and this, " and --
There won't be anything (unintelligible).

So they snuck on back to New York, and we finished out the week. And I brought in to cope with this Shelley Mann situation -- that's when Shelley Mann came in the band. So they came in for a week, and then it turned out Shadow got zonked out and so Shelley stayed.
So did the other people ever come back then?

The people who'd been in the band? Yeah, sure, they came back and finished up the whole thing, as we had originally planned to do. But I could see the problems as far as themselves and their people and their friends, but mainly, it was -- if you want to do some propaganda, this was not the band to do it with, I don't think.
Because we were integrated, it was not (unintelligible).
Yeah, sure, sure.
It's just that Love's Incorporated was not integrated.
Yeah. How about talking a little bit about Bill Harris? Since he also [arranged for] several of your Herds, too.
He which?
Bill Harris. Such a key figure...

Oh, without a doubt. He's certainly one of the one or two or three most outstanding people that ever went through our band. I guess I'd have to put him right there naturally with -- I think probably the best soloist, as far as going through more time periods with the different groups and the whole thing.

He certainly deserves to be the number one guy, because he fit everything I ever got involved in, and it just worked out -- and once again, we had a great communication thing, a great understanding of each other's desires and needs and he was extremely helpful to me in anything I was involved in. And it was a great loss, because he was a very warm human being, and in the same league with the Ralph Burns and many other people at that time.
His approach to the music and everything was mature when he arrived in the band.

Yeah, that's right. Well, he had been through some painful kinds of frustrating situations prior to joining us. As a growing man with a family, he was a meter reader with the Philadelphia Gas Company.
He was?

That was his gig. And he used to go around and play a little here and there on weekends, and jam. And then he went to audition for a band I guess he liked at the time, and another guy, a lead trombone player, he was
auditioning for the other chair. And the lead trombone player told the leader that he didn't have a good tone, said he didn't have a good tone, they couldn't use him.
(Laughter.)

And these kind of frustrating things happened to him. He never got over it, either, very sensitive person. And he would often bring up this guy's name, the bandleader's name, and say some snide remark.
I see.
He paid a lot of dues before he ever met me. In and out of all sorts of things. Bands like Bob Chester.
Oh, yeah.

And then, of course, the last commitment he had was with Benny Goodman when he did this[movie.] But evidently he had heard what we were getting into or something, because he was waiting to make the move.
He was?
Yeah.
He certainly gave the band -- among others, but I'm particularly thinking about him -- a very distinctive sound because of his solos.
And he did something which I think was truly remarkable. I'd never witnessed this anywhere, ever, before or since. He took two very competent trombonists, but
really with no feeling for jazz particularly, or -- they could play the trombone, let's leave it that way, and it doesn't matter who they were because that's not the import of this.

But at least once every couple of weeks, Bill would come to me and say, "Man, we got to get some trombone players. We ain't making it. These guys are driving me crazy." So I'd give him the same stock answer. "Bill, who do you want? Just give me their names, we'll call them, we'll hire them, all right?"
An hour later he'd come back to me and say, "Oh, man, forget what I said. We can't -- those are good guys." Are you ready for this? It was the fact that they were his bosom buddies.
Oh, uh-huh, uh-huh.
It was a constant battle.
Really.

From day to day, week to week. And the amazing thing out of all of it is the fact that he'd had these guys playing so far above their heads, from what they could normally do, that it was unbelievable. They sounded like -- three guys sounded like a five-trombone section.
Was he like this even through the late '50s, when he came back and did another --
Always.
Always.
Interesting.

And he loved to rib people. He had a wild sense of humor. Everything from slapstick to more sophisticated levels. But it's -- he was a very funny man and a very kind and warm man. Well, some of his better escapades was having life-size dummies in the trombone section.
(Laughter.)

He and Red Norvo wound up with these two lifesize dummies which were part of an act. Some people they'd run across, and there were a dancer who worked with these dummies. So they outfitted -- well, at least, Bill, the one he ended up with, he outfitted him with another band uniform. And he had him sitting next to him in the trombone section, with a horn propped there. And argued with him all night on the stand.
(Laughter.)
"Man, I told you to come in."
Oh, that's funny. Those are good things to recall.
Yeah, marvelous.
You have other things like that? I'm sure there's a potful of them.
Yeah, oh, I know. Well, in his more milder moments, he'd get in an elevator and -- in Chicago one

one day, he dropped his pants as he was leaving. He loved that kind of humor. And at one point, he had me calling some guy who was no longer -- evidently was not still around, but he was a man in Philadelphia who he had heard about, who had originally made cleats that went into the stages, and you could buy these shoes that comics would get, big shoes and they'd fit into the cleats and you could lean forward or lean back, or make some wild moves.
And I tried desperately for months to find this guy to make him a set of cleats. And he had it all worked out, how he was going to play //Everywhere// or something, and do that.
Oh, I see.
He said, 'Oh, that'll be amazing.'
What did you consider the most remarkable solo piece, because he did so many of them.

Yeah, well, I think he reached one of his high points, as far as the approach and the piece, the way it was written for him by Ralph, was 'Byou'. And I think it was a masterpiece what the way he played, it, as far as -- for the piece itself.
Then that became a model for some of the other imitators.
Well, sure. Well, he was probably the most imitated guy during that short period of his career of anyone in the whole trombone scene standard. He was the next big
move after.-- and until Bill showed up on the scene, as far as I was concerned, there were two trombone sounds, Tommy Dorsey and Jack Teagarden, one or the other.
And he was the first person to come along, to me, that had a whole different sound. He didn't sound like either of them.
Good.
And I think that's why -- that was one of the reasons that he started a whole new culture in his fashion.
Yeah, he did. Can we talk a little bit about Billy Bauer? Because -- yeah.
Well, he was a very unusual guy, a very inhibited man.
Huh.

Oh, yeah, very. And the only time he gave out was in his music. But everything else, he was very in himself and he had complexes and things. For awhile, while we were (inaudible) touring theatres, he said there was a guy following the band around, kept sitting in the balcony.
Yeah?

Who was trying to get his gig. And he kept saying, 'Man, you ain't making it. Now, you don't really play' you know. So we used to worry about Billy. But he was full of ideas and some of the earliest sounds we did, like, some of
the small group things, like "Four Men On A Horse," (inaudible).
Those are gems.
Now, he left you and then went back to work and study with Lennie Leonard Tristano.
Yeah, that's right. And he's still playing. He's still around New York. And I run into him once in awhile. As a matter of fact, we had him at the 40th anniversary.
Oh, yes, 40th anniversary.
That's the first time -- he I used to be out with an ice the night show or something, traveling just -- getting into the wierdest things.
I think -- what was the youngest player you recruited? Conte Candoli?

Yeah, well, every summer -- yeah, he just played during the summer for that first -- and we put him at fifth at the end of the line. And then when he graduated a year later (inaudible) come and join us.
He was like a little Gillespie-ite.
Yeah. But then that was so relevent a then to everybody. The mold had been set.
Yeah. Did he come before Pete?
No, Pete was there.
Pete was there early, wasn't he?
Yeah.
Well, both of them are doing well,
apparently.
Oh, yeah.
Pete's in San Francisco this week. Let's see, I'd like to ask you about Red Norvo, the last one, because he's still very active.

Which I'm very pleased about because he had some difficult problems a few years ago, with his hearing and everything. But I think that he has survived it, and evidently through some help, an operation, things have worked out that he's able to play again and hear what he needs to hear.
Well, there weren't that many people playing that way on his instrument, when you had him. And so I was interested in --

Well, in the first place, Red's probably had the longest career of anybody yet, because when he was very young he was with the Whiteman band and all that, then he had his own band, and he did many other things. He was involved in many things, because he was a showmanly person for one reason, and then the fact he had this impeccable taste as a musician.

And he was another time machine, in this way. A person that -- you can't upset him, you can't shake him one way or the other. He's like Davey in that respect. When you get a few of those people together, you can do some pretty fantastic things.
He has an unshakeable time feel. Well, I think -- the combination, the chemistry and so forth that these personalities --
Oh, that makes -- that's why some things will just be able to go beyond what you would be able to do with some other people. It's the individuals and that communication, and that feeling.
Well, was it -- at the end of this group's kind of period with you that you retired temporarily for awhile?

Yeah. And that lasted about seven months. We had just moved into this house and I wanted to see about -- I felt it was something I owed my family, and way overdue, and something I wanted to do. And I came, and I lasted seven months.
I see.
Then I heard a trumpet player by the name of Ernie Royal, and that started --
The ball rolling again.
Yeah.
Let me ask you this. When did you meet Charlotte now? Was it in San Francisco?
Yes, we met in San Francisco when we were both extremely young, and she was there working in a show.
As a dancer.
Working in North Beach Palladium.
Was she a dancer -- wasn't she?
Well, she basically worked as an actress, later doing straight work and doing comedy.
You were with Tom Garen's band at the time?
Yeah. And that's how we met, and then we started an association. At least, we kept in touch with each other. On the road for a period of time, for years, actually. And about six years later --
When did you get married then? What year was that?
The year was 1936, September of '36. And we started the band -- our first job was November, 1936. So we were married a couple of months while we were rehearsing, and recording.
I see. So she began with your -- actually your leadership career.
Yes, that was -- our marriage and the band kind of side by side. Forty-two years.
And when did your daughter come into this world? Ingie.
I think it's '42.
I see. I ask these questions so that it will fit back into why you were thinking about your family.
So she was a little over four years old.
Yeah. And that's the reason I wanted to be home, to (inaudible) together for awhile.
So you heard Ernie Royal.
Yeah.
Where and how did that come about? Live? Did you hear him live?
Yeah, I heard him in a little group down on Sunset Boulevard. Very talented guy, arranger, songwriter, material writer, pianist. Phil Moore --
Oh, Phil Moore.

-- had a little group, and Ernie and his brother Marshall, and I forget who he's the drummer in the rhythm section. But when I hired heard Ernie, and he was playing exclusively in a Harmon mute and a cup mute, when I heard him and what he could do with such ease, I decided to get me a band.
(Laughter.)
Now, how did you generate this new edition of the band?
Well, I just asked him if he wanted to come join, and he said, 'Yeah, that sounds all right.' So I said, 'Well, I'll put together a band then.' And I got some of the people back.
Yes.
And Ralph came out to help me put it
together and then we got Jimmy Giuffre Duke who showed up to write a including, couple of things, and the Four Brothers, and we were on our way.
Yeah, well, let's --
We went ahead and did some records right away.
So this -- the Four Brothers sound started with Jimmy experimenting in some little place on the East Side, here, didn't it?

Yeah, down on the beach, too, the guys were fooling around. But he wasn't the only one. As a matter of fact, there were other people involved in experimenting with it, four tenors sometimes, or three tenors and a baritone or whatever. They needed to get away from the usual.
Yeah. There was a name of a place -- I can't remember the name, it starts with a P, Petracelli's or --
Yeah.
What is it?
Something like that.
Something like that, yeah. That was where it happened.
Yeah, I guess so, (unintelligible).
Yeah, uh-huh. Now, did somebody refer that whole concept to you that he was --
Oh, they wanted me to hear it.
Oh, they did?

Yeah. So then, -- and then Herbie Steward was an alto player. We would (unintelligible) saxophone sections, which we did. Sam Marowitz came back, and so, like, -- but I did say, I did hire Serge Chaloff, because I heard about him, and I figured he'd be a good -- he'd be the right baritone for that period.

And then when Getz and Zoot and -- and Sam had tried to hold these guys together as far as the section was concerned, and he didn't have too much trouble, and Herbie Stewart was a good little alto player.
Right.
But he also had played tenor, so in order to let me hear this sound, they played a few other things.
So did Jimmy bring this thing over to you to --
Later he brought the piece, yeah.
Oh, but the sound itself, --
Yeah, they had been experimenting with it, by themselves, yeah.
With different kinds of music, then, you had heard it before the "Four Brothers" per se.
Yeah, but it was the first thing that was written for us, using that sound.
Yeah.
Actually, the guy who did most of the experimentation was not available to me nor was I even aware of him. But it was a guy that used to work with Kenton, and an arranger.
Pete Rugolo?
No.
No?
No.
Before him? Or after?
Well, it was during. He was one of the trumpet players, and didn't play much trumpet, but --
Ray Wetsel?
No.
No.
No, this guy still arranges. Then he would come back every so often and write again for Kenton. He did those things like -- I think --

Oh, I see.

Yeah. Ralph was writing while we were rehearsing, and all this sort of thing. I see.
Or from somebody like Jack Teagarden's big band.
