No, he was just recommended to me.
Oh, he was recommended to you.
Yes.
I see. Because at that time they were all kind of in that same mode.
Yeah, that's it, and they were all unknown guys. You only knew them, like, -- the same reputations I hear about young players every day in the same way.
Yeah, I see.
'And there's a guy from -- used to be around New York, or he was in Philadelphia. He's out here now, and his name is Stan Getz.'
I see. Okay. In that band, now, what did you feel was significantly exciting compared with the first one? It had its own brand of excitement and had some of the carry-overs, some of the key people.
Yeah. The carryover people, with rare exceptions, came back later. In other words, the first band did not have Bill Harris or Chubby. But it did have Sam Stan in lead alto and --
And Earl Swope.
Yeah, we had Earl Swope in that, and a guy I just saw for the first time in years recently, Ollie--
Mitchell?

Ollie Mitchell. No, not Ollie Mitchell, (Wilson) it's a different guy's name. Ollie -- and he was from Washington, D.C. When we needed replacements or were looking for people, we got a lot of guys from Washington.
From Washington?
Yeah, for some reason. Don Lamond and these guys. It's his hometown.
Oh, I see.
So that's how Swope got there, it's how -- we all kind of suggested people.
Yeah. Well, I think it's interesting to find out where these centers of recruitment have been, and these little pools of talent.
Yeah, they looked (inaudible) everywhere.
Yeah. Now, in this band, you brought in Terry Gibbs, didn't you?
Yeah, he came -- he had been with Tommy
Dorsey for a short time. And I heard about him -- he had been suggested and I heard about him, and brought him in. He joined the band in Milwaukee. I think we were doing theaters.
This band was much more hard pop oriented, it seems to me.

Oh, yeah, because we were in the very early stages of just being involved somewhat in bop in the first band, I would think. Then the second band was really based on the bop feeling, and we left our audience lots of times wondering what we were into. But I figured we had to go through all the moods.

Did -- now, you still had the Columbia contract then, before you moved over to Capitol. So the significant things, "Summer Sequence" and all that, were still on here. Can you talk about how that came about with Ralph? Did he just come to you with it, or --
"Summer Sequence?"
Yeah.
No, we had first done the first three movements of it at our first jazz concert in '46.
That's that MGM thing that was [deleted].
Yeah, and then we didn't get around to doing it again until '47, '48.
I see.
And then he wrote the fourth movement
for it, which later turned out to be "Early Autumn." (unintelligible).
But Getz was already in the band.
Yeah. But was that just by some quirk of assignment, here, you, Stan, take the solo for Early Autumn, or did you really feel that --
No, when he wrote it as Early Autumn, he wrote it for Stan.
Oh, he had him in mind.
Yeah.
So he had already --
But Ralph had heard the sound of what he was writing for in the fourth movement.
I see.
You know, the developments and as Ollie played it the trombone came very pretty clearly on that fourth movement.
So when did some of the other guys come back? Was it after --

It was after -- actually we were running into obstacle courses with bookings and so on. And one thing led to another and -- well, the late Carlos Gaselle took over the personal management of the band, and he was the one who was obsessed with the idea that he had to have two or three of the people back who were in the original band.
And when he asked me whom I thought I would like or
who I could get, at this point, that's when Bill Harris came back and Chubbie, and I guess everybody.
(Interruption)
Ernie Royal had -- now we're going to get into the names again. This is that period for me, that --
Yeah, Al Porcino? Persino?
No. No, we had like all legit players. I'll have to get this --
Oh, it's probably right in that Columbia Thundering Herds. We'll get it.
(Recording interrupted.)
(Inaudible.)
Which one? Well, there's a couple of sections. You have Stan Fishelson. Bernie Glow. Ernie Glow.
Ernie Glow actually was the lead player.
Shorty, Irv Markowitz, and Ernie Royal, yeah. That's quite a section.
Right. Ernie had already left the band then.

Uh-huh. This was Summer Sequence, yeah, "I Told Ya Ya" "I Love You, Now Get Out." That I remember because (inaudible) "Keen and Peachy," "The Goof and I," was the same time. "Geefin' Eye," and "I've Got News For You." Yeah.
Okay, well, anyway, what was the reception like for with this band, of people who knew you were away and here comes another Herd. How did you get the word "Herd?"
Well, the 'Herd' had been in use from '45 on.
Yeah.

And, of course, that began and was used as a way of describing our music. George Simon said he thought that the band sounded like a thundering herd. And so we just kept that as billing. And the reception to the second band was certainly not as spontaneous as the first one was. And there were some very uphill battles. People said they couldn't dance to it where it was necessary, and --
I see.

But this was also -- I base a lot of this on the fact that the band business was over. That's really what I base it on, because at the end of 1946, that was the end. If you just look at the passing of bands, who left the business during that period, it was like a complete fallout. So it was a big drought happening, and then trying to experiment at a time like that, you're going to really run into a stone wall.
Uh-huh, and make a comeback at the same time.

Yeah, right. Maybe -- I'm sure I'd had a much easier time of it if I had just gone back with what I had been doing, or even somewhat of a facsimile. But coming up with something brand new and something they hadn't heard,
it was very difficult. different.

Tell me, even though you began with the original motivation and interest, because you heard Ernie Royal, how did you conceptualize this direction of being innovative in some sense here, and incorporating many of the things that were in the forefront of the music? Was that part of when you were reorganizing it? Did you rethink about --
No, no. I think --
It just developed.
These things are not planned, not in my case, at least. No, no, I can't have a big psyching out session and then go ahead and do it.
Yeah, yeah.
Now, a lot of my experimentation, 99 percent of the time has been done on the bandstand, and it's a very natural kind of thing.
Was the work still very much available out there for you?

No, it was getting touchier and touchier, more difficult all the time. And along with all the other problems, it was difficult. And that's why I eventually just stopped the band, that one, because we ran out of gas, from every aspect.
The band was not producing what it should have musically, I didn't feel, because we were now concerned with drugs
and so on. So we -- there were multiple kinds of things happening that we were all kind of helping to start a dis-integration period.
When did you cut it off?

Well, what I did, rather than just have a dead cutoff, I put a closing time on the band which I think was December or something, and went home for Christmas, and then immediately after put together a small group and went to Cuba for a month. And the small group included Shelly Manne, Ralph Burns on piano, Red Mitchell on bass, Conte Candoli, Milt Jackson, and that's it -- oh, yeah, and Dave Barber.
Oh, really?
Yeah. After I put the group together, he called and said he'd like to go to Cuba. So I said, 'Well, sure, come on.'
This was --
Right.
And when did you get -- was Carlos still involved?
Yeah, and he booked that trip.
How long was that sojourn?
A month we were there. We stayed in the -- it was a location for a month.
Oh, it was a location.

Yeah. Then I went back to New York and started to reorganize again. I think I took a rest for a little bit, but it was shortly after. And then that would be the band where we started with the three tenors and baritone exclusively.
Al Cohn
And so Hal Cohen was there and Zoot.
So you're still on Columbia then, for a while.
No.
No? You moved to Capitol?
We were on Capitol with all that.
Yeah.
"Music for Dancing" and all that stuff.
Yeah.
That was Capitol.
Yeah.
Then after Capitol we went with MGM for a short time.
Well, that was -- let's see, now, it was at Capitol when you brought in Nat. Is that the first time that he had -- when he was in the -- some of the road bands? Ralph Burns was still writing.
[George]
Yeah, still writing for me. But Nat came in sometime during that period, early '50s.
Yeah.
I think Nat joined the band in New Orleans when we were at the Roosevelt Hotel. I don't remember.
Had you had contact with him before, or was he another --
No, he was recommended to me, I think by Ralph and a couple of guys.
I see.
From Berklee in Berkeley and Boston. That became the Boston contingent.
I see, I see. Because he told me, oh, within the last few months that he was very heavy into playing bebop, which I didn't really know, because I always thought he was playing basic things.
I think he thought he was playing bebop.
Yeah. (Inaudible.) Well, did he start to write for you shortly after joining the band?
Yeah, yeah.
And what was the relationship with him, because he was another --
Oh, we got along fine, and had no problems of any kind, really. And he's a very prolific writer. He could sit down and write five arrangements and come in with them, and run them down and we'd go.
And he was very big influence in that '60s band,

there's no doubt about it. And he was of great import, and he had a free hand. He had a free hand to hire people like Bill Holman to help him write for the band. And he always had impeccable taste, so he hired people like Bill Holman.

And so he did a big job for us, and then he stayed with me through a lot of different situations. And now, when he talked to me, today, which is very interesting, he played this new album because Nat had called him. He'd played it or something. And it sounds very much like our band of the '60s, which is fine.
That is correct.
But, this has the same problems that everyone has, and I try desperately not to have, and that is simply to try to do something almost as good as you did. This is very difficult.
Oh, yeah, to emulate yourself.
Yeah, it's rough.
Well, he is one of the people that have been with your organization off and on for many years.
Many years, probably longer than anybody. We figured it out one time, that he was in and out of the band for a period of 12 to 15 years, somewhere in there.
That's a long time.
Yes, it is, in any man's league.
He also assumed the role of road manager.
Which almost turned into disaster.
Yes. I remember, he had a few jobs. Well, he's very much associated with you in many ways.
Oh, definitely, definitely.

Wonder if you would want to expand on that, because he is one of the key people here. We'd like to have some more information on what you feel about how he assisted you and if he did musically or supervisory or whatever.

Well, I don't think -- in fact, I'm sure I couldn't have done nearly what we did with the '60s band if he hadn't been there constantly and to be overseeing it and so on.

I had a lot of great talent there, and they would rather have played a lot of different kinds of music that we were doing at the time. Sometimes I lost the talent, sometimes I didn't. But I think that the reason it was reasonably successful is because it was limited to music that Nat was producing for us.
So for that time, it was really appropriate.

Absolutely, most appropriate. And I think that that was some of the best music that those guys could play at the time. That's why it's a high point. I think there's a high point in each period, if you happen to be lucky enough to be in on it, kiss it and say goodbye.
He was with you, now, in the '50s when you had your own label you were trying to, Mars.
Well, I'd say it was Howie Richmond's label, but I was involved.
Whose label?
Howie Richmond.
Howie Richmond, I see.
Yeah, a very successful music publisher.
Oh, I see. How did that come down? He asked you to front it?

Well, he had been a press agent for me many years and many years ago, and actually, when we came back from the '54 tour in Europe, with that band, Bill Perkins and people like that, Nat was on that tour and on that trip Johnny Howell and people -- Howie, this friend of mine, heard the band, and we'd had a successful European tour. And he said, 'Boy, this band should make some records right now, it's really ripe.' And I said, 'Fine.'

So he got everybody -- somebody, I should say, at Columbia steamed up, and we went over and made a session. And we were all pleased with it. And -- but a strange thing had happened at Columbia. There was now a new head of the pop and jazz and everything department. And I think everyone knows that it was Mitch Miller.
And Mitch Miller just made one comment on hearing
the tape, that he didn't find it exciting.
Really?
So he speaks for -- that's how he started the label. And we released that first date immediately.
So you had those on -- weren't they ten-inchers?
Yes.
Ten-inch copies originally?
Yeah.
How long did that last? That company?
Oh, probably a year and a half.
Short-lived.

But there was a very sensible reason for it stopping. It became a real chore for Howie Richmond because he was not a record man to begin with. He was an extremely successful businessman, but he ran into an obstacle that he had never really heard of before, and that was independent distributors, where you send out the records and make the investment and then never get your money back.
And so, he was devoting more time to trying to get the monies than -- it just wasn't worth the bother. But fortunately he was able to sell the whole thing to Norman Granz.
Right.
Who did nothing with it, but kept it long enough to sell it to MGM -- back to MGM again.
Of course, those records were available for --
Yeah, that's right. We had pretty good distribution for the times.
Yeah, yeah, I thought so.
Yeah. And I think we did produce some pretty decent records.
You had some great guys in that band -- Carl Fontana --
That was a whole different grouping again.
Yeah. Did you have Phil Urso, too?

For a short period, yeah. That was the band that once again, Perkins and a lot of different guys. And Doug Mettome, marvelous trumpet player and a young man that -- from Minnesota, another great trumpet player, it's a Nordic name and I can't think of it. Don Fagerquist.
Don Fagerquist.

Marvelous player. So it's hard to -- so, like, when people say to me, 'What was your best band,' this was a very difficult question in my case, because I think each one of those bands had something to say, and I think we did it the best we could with what we had to offer, and I think it was great for the time. And that's my only argument, and that's not a cri-

tique as far as Nat or anyone else, who tries to dwell where it was. I have a thing now I say at the end of certain tunes we do, "and that's the way it was." That we should distinguish it from -- that's not the way it is.
Good, good. Woody, what about the principal radio shows you had in earlier days? You had a couple of them, didn't you, cigarettes and Wildroot Cream Oil and --

Yeah. Well, the first one, actually, was -- the first one that we had a series, a matter of weeks, was Old Gold cigarettes, and it was an incongruous mating, I think. It was our band along with a former movie singer and actor, the guy that did -- was famous for Donkey Serenade, Allen Jones.
Oh, Allen Jones.

Yes. So, he was a kind of legit singer, and with a jazz band it really was kind of a strange mating. As a matter of fact, the original premise of the show was, I think, his vocals and the band of Frankie Carl, the pianist. And for some reason or other, maybe it was because some record of ours was selling, -- I'll never know the reason, actually, but we wound up on the show and it turned out pretty well. And it wasn't too much later, in the following season, we finally got our complete own show and that was for the Wildroot Cream Oil hair dressing. And we did about 13 weeks, I think. And then, when we concluded our stint, Nat Cole took
took over the show with the trio.
Now, both of these were network shows.
Yes.
What year was that first one?
'44, I believe, and the next one was '45.
Uh-huh. That's how Wildroot came around.
Wildroot travelled with us, which made it very -- it was a great thing for the band. Once a week, and it emanated from wherever we were.
All right. Let's jump back out to the '50s for a moment. You had a major tour, didn't you, for the State Department to South America?
Yes, we went to South American in 1958, and it was a very lengthy tour, about three and a half months.
Three and a half months.
Yeah.
Was that your first one out of the country?
No.
On a State Department kind of --

For the State Department, yes. And it was an interesting tour. However, unfortunately our State Department people, at least during that period, were not very well equipped to get the most good out of having someone like
ourselves there. They didn't really know how to --
Capitalize.
-- approach it from an impresario department. And so very often, we'd go for a week and maybe do one concert in a whole week.
Is that right?
Yeah.
Wow.
Of course, that made it an interesting tour.
Was this the one -- did you have Tito Puente down there at all? Was he down there at all?
No. No, all my association with Tito has been in New York.
I see. Now, you were then under contract with Everest Records?
Yeah, we had a (inaudible) with them, yes. And we did some interesting things. We redid 'Summer Sequence.'
Charlie Byrd?
And we even redid 'Ebony Concerto.'
Uh-huh, that's right.

And speaking of 'Ebony Concerto,' I think you might be interested in this. They've asked me to see if we can't perform it at a Stravinsky festival in Holland in 1980, and I said that I would certainly like to do it, but that I
would probably prevail on someone like Buddy DeFranco to play the clarinet solo, because I don't have the time to prepare for it, and it would take a lot of time at my stage of the game.
But I think we'll do it.
Well, that's right. That'll be a wonderful experience and contribution.
I just thought I'd throw that in.
Yeah, it's a good one, it's a good one. You haven't talked to Buddy about it, have you?

I haven't yet, because this happened only a month ago and I only spoke to the man who's in charge. And he was at an engagement -- I played in Holland and he was so impressed with the group and so on, and he asked -- he knew -- he had heard about the Stravinsky piece.
Do you recall the preliminary discussions about your going on the State Department tour, the one to South America, how that had come about?
It was done pretty much through an official booking service. It really had no personal contact with me whatsoever.

However, in my estimation, it was pretty much a success because we were able to in some areas do something towards -- for the reason that we were really there. If you have a long memory, you might remember that there was a Nixon
affair in -- where he was spat upon by students and young people in -- I think it was Venezuela.

And that's where we opened our tour. And however, Niagara, I think the interesting thing about it was that the State Department sent over our band for jazz, they sent over the New York Philharmonic with two conductors, [Leonard] Bernstein and [Dmitri] Metropolis, and the San Francisco Ballet and the Catholic University drama group from Washington. And we were all at different times in different areas of South America.
Oh, I see.
We covered almost all of it, and so did the other people.
I've never heard anything --
It was quite expansive, yeah.
Yeah.
And it had to do with the Nixon affair.
I see.

And then, in our case, we were able to -- they were quite a bit ahead of us as far as student uprisings and different situations. And we were able in a couple of situations to, I think, be helpful for our image, the United States image, inasmuch as -- it was an architectural university, I forget now if it was in Venezuela or if it was in Chile.
But it was a university, it had been on strike for
months. And there were pickets and there was no entrance and so on. But they let us in and allowed people to come hear us play.
I'll be darned.
Yeah. Which I thought was pretty --
Did you find any sizeable group of people that were very familiar with your music?
Not in South America.
Not in South America. I just was curious about that.
All over the rest of the world, where we had visited, at --
Sure, yeah.
South America's very strange.
I think it's mainly because they have their own music and are very closely tied to it.
So the '50s really was more of a probing period, trying to survive.
Trying to survive, actually.
Right, survive --
Very difficult period.
You had -- I recall, when you came out to the Monterey Jazz Festival, and you did that live album for Atlantic, that was a group that was kind of put together out there --
Just for -- just put together just for
the Festival. Some of my guys from New York came back with me, [Bill] including Chase and so on. But actually, it was supposedly an all-star group, and so --
Yeah. Well, you had a lot of alumni members in it.
Yeah, a few, and also people that really had no association with me at all, but were there for obvious reasons, like Sy Zentner, and for even less obvious reason was Mel Lewis.
Oh, yeah? That was his first with you.
It's the only time we ever worked together, ever.

Just speaking about festivals of the past, it seems like it's countless now, the number of festivals (inaudible) you've been around. And even starting in the '50s, you were pretty active. You were out here, I think, in one memorable one I recall that had Roy Eldridge, Ben Webster, Earl Hines --
That's right, yes, I was.
Anyway, that was -- you have made appearances by yourself and with your own band, other peoples' bands, just a variety of contexts.

I heard a tape not too long ago that was sent to me by a friend, Joe McDonald in San Francisco, a drummer. He worked with me for a short period of time, and was a good friend of Bill Paul Harris'. And they arranged -- the Arts

or society Society did a think in Boston on the Commons with the local hot players, and I fronted the band and we did some of our charts, and he sent me a tape, and it sounded remarkably good. I was really amazed.
It was a one-shot.
When was this?
Well, this would be during that '50s period.
During that period.
Yeah.
Okay, well, if -- do you have anything else to say about that period, the decade of the '50s?
No, but anyone who survived it should be congratulated.
Should be congratulated. You then went through a number of recordings, too. You have one on the Jazzland.
Well, they usually were things that were recorded for some other reason. Someone would --
Nat and Adderly was on it, yeah. In closing the '50s --
(Recording interrupted.)
Why don't we go on to following the close of the decade of the '50s. Things start to happen again in the '60s for you.
Well, it was a very strange beginning,

because I once again was running out of gas. And I took a small group on the road. But I managed to hang out to what -- my key personnel in this small group, as far -- and it was a strange kind of small-group thing because it was like an act. But I kept the players that I felt I needed at the time, and that was Nat in the rhythm section, and the same rhythm section we had had in the band a little earlier. And I kept Bill Chase with me and I kept a tenor player, Gordon -- [Pierce]
Brisker?
Brisker. And so at least if we could get in and out of things, if we needed to have a band in 20 minutes, we could do something.
Uh-huh.
Because it was really tough then to get bookings and so on, and yet, that was the beginning of the '60s band, right there.

So -- and I think what really put the '60s band -- I know what put it together, was the Metropolis. And the fact that it took a lot of responsibilities off of me. The salaries of the band and so on were paid by this place. And I was given actually a salary, that simply would take care of my immediate needs.
Yeah.
And we could pick and choose a time, if we got some good dates, we could go out for two weeks or four
weeks, and come back and go back in for two or four weeks, or whatever we wanted.
Wow.
It was -- otherwise, I don't think that band could have been built at that time. I don't think there was that kind of interest or --
How --

And it was a great place to break in a band, by sheer necessity, because you either played together or you'd never see each other again, being in a police lineup above a bar or playing into a mirror for a baffle.
Like a firing squad, really.
That's right, yeah. But it really worked into a remarkable quick way to get a band in shape.
Was that '61 and '62?
Along in there, yeah.
In there?
Yeah, and--
You had that Sea-Sack record in there, in December of '62, that band, and I was just wondering whether that was before.
No, that -- the Sea-Sack thing was done, actually, with another Allstar group, some of the guys, --
Yeah, you'd have to (unintelligible).
Right.
But, so, what you're talking about pre-dated --
Yes.
Okay.
And then, of course, I think another thing that made it all possible was, in the midst of this whole scene, I went in with the rhythm section and did a quartet album for Phillips.
Right, yeah.

And it was the first successful album we'd had in several years, as far as sales went and so on, and it played. And from that, I was able to convince them, because we were now in the Metropole, that they should record a big band. They had no eyes to, just -- most labels didn't at that period.
Yeah.
But they went ahead with it, and that was one of the earliest things in '63, and "Encore" of '63.
Now, the band that you had in the Metropole during this time, were most of those people on the first album, with Phillips, most of them?
Most of them, yes.
Was Phil Wilson there, at the time?
On this 1963 album?
No. Prior to the album.
Oh, yeah, they were there for some time, yeah.
Yeah. I'm just wondering who was in there,because this is a gap that I haven't heard too much about.
No, well, I guess there is no way you can really check on it. No, I think pretty much the band was pretty much intact.
Really.
Sal Nistico was there, through the whole scene. Some of the --
Chuck Andrus, he was --
He was -- the same rhythm section, constantly.
Because he had that quartet date with you.
Yeah. And, of course, --
Jake?

Jake was there, constantly, and Nat Pierce and Chase was there every night, through the whole -- and if we got different trumpet players at different times, they were usually guys from Boston or New York area, who'd been in the band, or -- that was his department. And then the trombones, it was sometime during that earliest time, when we brought in a guy from Richmond, Virginia --
Henry Southall?
Yeah, Henry.
Uh-huh.
And, of course, the other chair was many different people we had hired.
Many people, yeah.
And the same baritone saxophonist who was with the band all through the '60s, from Boston also, passed away last year.
Really?
Yeah. Little short --
Oh, you mean Tom Anastis? Anastas?
That's right, Tommy Anastis. Anastas.
Yeah.
He was in that band.

And we had some very high points with that band, because during the -- at some given point we wound up doing a tour of Europe, and it was by far and away, at that point, the most successful tour we had had, and we did some British television for BBC that really upset everybody, because the band was very -- it was at a peak.
Was that the occasion when the musicians shut down from whatever they were doing, and they all ended up at this place that to hear -- the band?
Right, yeah.
Yeah, I heard about that. And it was

really an exciting time, but once again, about every time you get to the bottom of the barrel, then something would happen and they'd start another group or the group gets revived or whatever you want to call it.
Yeah.
It was an exciting time.
Well, this group had -- once again, another incredible combination of terrific players.
Yeah, exactly.
For that time.
Right.
Pete. Peaked. You had Nat writing for you once again, there. It was quite a bit of material, it seemed to me.

And he was taking things which ordinarily -- put into the concept, maybe they wouldn't have been done by as many people, if we hadn't first gotten into it. Oh, we were into some of the early things, in other words, Horace Silver.
Horace Silver? Yeah, Charlie Mingus.
Charlie Mingus.
Charlie Right.
Charlie We did Mingus things and we were getting into a lot of -- and Nat would dig up these things.
I see.
And A border "Watermelon Man" was
Herbie Hancock.
Right, right.
So he was very alert and very aware, and he had his ear to the ground. And so that was probably -- was his most valuable time in any group that we had, his most valuable time.
Oh, I see, through the many editions he's been with you.
Right, right.
That one really --
Well, of course, looking back, too, that was clearly the time when people related to Nat's contributions more than ever, too.
Yes.
And he did things with standards, too, that were beautiful arrangements.
Oh, yeah, standards, and we'd do pop tunes. If Necessary, but they were all in a typical swinging fashion.
Uh-huh.
And all of a sudden, people would begin to understand us, again, for the 19th time.
Yeah, well, it was very exciting, because as you know, I was a little more tuned in to that edition than some of the other ones.
Yeah. And, of course, I think when we came to hit the coast with it the first time, at Basin Street West in L.A., --
Oh, yes.
And we just -- the Encore album, there.
Right.
And I don't think there was anybody in this town who didn't become aware of the band.
Right, right, it was hot.
Everybody from Nat Cole to Henry Mancini was there while we were recording this album live.
Yeah, that was exciting for you, I remember. That was just before you came up here to the Basin Street West (inaudible) here.
Right.

Yeah. Why don't we talk a little bit about some of the key people in this band, because it was, like, people were saying, 'my gosh, it's like we haven't heard another one like this since the First Herd.' You remember, all the talk that was going on.
Oh, yeah.
So it was heralding another era.
Yeah, but I think this has been a productive period from '69 on, as far as producing, once again, -- what I hope would be another approach and another way. We'd
gotten into the composer's music of this period, which is Chick Corea Correa and many others.
Oh, yeah, of course.

But I think that it's been a good period, because once again I wound up with some writing that's far and away the best of this period. I'm speaking now about people like Alan Broadbent and -- who I think did some phenomenal things. And being able to take an old piece of material, like Blues in the Night, and make it into something completely new and different, to me, that was a personal triumph for him and for me.
When Alan came in, that was really a continuation of the energy that was started by the early '60s band.
That's right.

You had an incredible inventory of guys going through '62, '63, '64, '65, '66 band, it was who were just fabulous. It seemed, too, that it was at that time that you had had one of the biggest influxes of people out of the colleges.

Well, that was the beginning, actually. The music schools were starting to give us new guys that we'd never seen the likes of before, because they could do things that, really, we hadn't even attempted yet. By that I mean their technical proficiency and the things we could attempt now were a little more above what we had been doing.
Yeah. Are you able to talk about some of those people? Because I know, as I recall, there were quite a number from Boston.
Yes, it was very highly represented.
Yeah, very much.

It would be interesting, I think, to some people, the fact too that Alan Broadbent for one was recommended very highly and had been heard and involved -- Nat Pierce was the first to tell me about him. And then George Shearing I heard from, telling me that he had heard this phenomenal young man. And so on. So he came very highly recommended.
Uh-huh.
And his writing had a great deal to do with where we started to move. And what I would attempt and what we would all attempt. And --
I can't remember the -- how long did Bill Chase stay with you?
Well, actually, during that period, or the early stages of that band, --
Yeah.
-- he was in Vegas.
Oh, yeah.
Doing financially very well. And he went through his show biz period and so on. And then, when I
felt that it was -- time was ripe for him to certainly get out of Vegas, that's when we worked it out for --
(End of Side One.)
The latter part of the 1950s, as I recall, he was in and out.
And I can't recall the year when he finally left, because I happened to be there at the time, in Vegas, when he decided to go.
Yeah, yeah. I think it would be around '69 or '70.
Maybe so, maybe a little earlier.
Yeah.
Anyway, he occupied a key role in that band, didn't he?
Oh, yes, definitely.
Can you talk a little bit about his contribution to your band? Aside from music, he did a lot of other things.

Yeah, well, he was always -- for one thing, we had a very close, warm association, he and I, just as guys. We had a lot of the same hobbies and the same things we enjoyed doing. Cars, automobiles, engines and things of that nature.
Yes.
And we'd both be sloshing around Europe or the United States, wherever we were, trying to catch a race or the Grand Prix or the Indianapolis or whatever. And so we
spent a lot of time in that fashion, which was the first time, actually, that anybody in my band and I got that tight, because we had mutual likes and hobbies.

And so we became -- and remained, very dear friends. And I think I encouraged him. I know I did, very strongly, about his own group and where I felt he should go and so on. So if anyone worried about the fact that his group was too far out and was too -- and that it was too electric, too involved with electronics, well, they better cut me in for half of it, at least, because I was -- any time he came up with a thought like that, I encouraged him beyond the call of duty. Because I felt he would have great appeal to the kids who were buying the records and buying the music.
Oh, yeah. No question about it, that it did happen.
Yeah, yeah.
When he was on your band, he was featured now and then, and played a key role in the trumpet section.
Oh, yeah. As a matter of fact, almost everything that -- as far as anything that came from the trumpet section was pretty much guided by where he wanted to go.
I think Jake has Javis mentioned that he would always have his ears with what Bill was doing, and vice versa, and they seemed to work as a very good team.
Oh, yeah, right. But in some respects,

you see, there were some things where I would have to feel that Bill and I were of certain similarities about the two of us, because where Jake and some of the other people didn't want to go to a new world, Bill and I had a perfect understanding of why we had to go to the new world.
Uh-huh.
Which I think explains the --
I understand now, because --
That didn't make us lose our feelings for the other people, but --
Oh, yeah.
We were going over there, anyway, see.
Yeah, uh-huh. I think I talked to him several times about Jake as a drummer, Jake Hanna, being kind of another peak for you as far as a drummer was concerned. Like Dave Tough.
Yeah, that's right.
Very selfless type of drummer. drumming.

Right. But, there again, I believe it was his peak also, and to this respect, he has never wanted to leave that feeling right there. That's where he -- and as a matter of fact, when we were first just experimenting, doing jazz waltzes and things, he got very bugged.
He doesn't dig those.
'' Yeah, man -- but these are these different individualistic situations.
Yeah, sure, sure.
The way people would play.
And another person associated with that edition, of course, is Sal Nistico. There are certain people that people won't ever forget.

That's right. Well, Sal Nistico was a dynamite player, as long as you'd give him a tempo, he'd play it. I don't think his sensitivities were as great as some of the other tenors we've had, but that's something else. For what he did, I don't think there was anyone ever any better, or maybe not nearly as good.
And -- but he also reached his peak with the rhythm section that he claimed he didn't like. And he would never have played those tempos, probably, with somebody else.
That's true. He didn't know what he had.
Yeah, that's right. But these are the things that a good coach has to be aware of, on how to keep people from jumping on each other when there's no need for it.
How did you handle things like that? I know that must have been --
I danced a lot.
There were a lot of interpersonal problems in that band, but like all of them do, I guess.
Yeah, sure. But usually, it wound up pretty good because I think that I used the right psychology
with most of them. Beyond a certain point, they were talking to themselves. And once you get this message, you don't want to go to that point. That's the way I feel about it.

You have another -- I don't want to forget this because it just crept into my mind. I've always observed with admiration how you program. Now, a lot of the bands, they are almost predictable from one set to the next. Yours -- you feel things, you seem to have antennae that people talk about, musicians talk about, other people. And they don't know what you're going to be calling until you do it.
Yeah.
And I don't know how you do it, but you must have some kind of pulse meter out there.
Well, I really don't -- how can you --
Not formal or anything, but you just --

Yeah. But it's something that I've been aware of since I was a child, really. Maybe -- it could very well have been the fact that I did play to audiences from the time I could remember, and anytime I think something is losing an audience, even for one second, I sense -- somehow I seem to feel this and to receive the message. And I'll do some very strange switches, sometimes, in midstream, but it usually works.
Uh-huh. This keeps everybody on their toes, too, though.
Yeah, well, because I don't like --
Let's face it.
Well, that becomes part of the challenge for them, too, and if they can anticipate it, why --
It is. I wonder if that maintains a kind of freshness for people beyond just the challenge per se, but just even how it's being put together as a whole.

Yeah, well, I think so, and then we open up things or we close them up, depending on how the reaction is moving and so on. Like, I won't often clip a guy down to two bars and say, you've had it. But another time there's room for opening up a thing and your audience will accept it and buy it, and -- or it's creating a very good feeling and a good mood or something. And another time, it would be a waste to give these people something they don't understand. It's too good for them, so we'll cut it off.

You, of course, like many people -- not many, I can't say that, bandleaders that have such a deep repertory, so many decades of experience, and a number of selections associated with you specifically. It gives you a breadth of material to choose from, whenever you want to. You would 'Laura' if you wanted to, or something that's -- you just did a week ago. And you can mix that up. And most people can't do that. And you don't do anything for nostalgia purposes, either, do you?
Well, I try not, but however, we're all
kind of guided by the people we're playing for, and if it's an older audience you're going to play other things that you would for --
Sure. I know, when you do a dance date, you have a lot of Nat Pierce's charts, "Deep Purple."
(Inaudible) leftovers. Is that okay with you guys?
It's up to Herb.
Sure.
Okay.
I can't take it, I'm going out.
(Laughter.)
Let's see. Oh, yeah, the programming even that you have today, you keep a certain basic library in your book, don't you? You call over periodically to take things out.
Yeah.
Shove it aside or keep it at home.
And that sometimes can be pretty hazardous, too, because about the time you take something out, then you have a call for it or something.
How many charts to you keep, on the average?
Too much, besides the guys who are doing the breakup and who put the band together. The weight is impossible and we have gigantic cases, and -- but, then, too,

we've been somewhat fortunate by being able to find our things once again, when we do -- for instance, before I went to Europe simply -- they asked that I do some things out of the '40s period, and we were able to rejuvenate them and fix them. And having the Woody Herman archives at the University of Houston has made this possible, and also, there's a lot of our material at Berklee that could be put to use again, and so on.
The ones down at University of Houston, are they on microfilm or are they actually --
No, they're music. It's actually -- they've fixed up a lot of it and cleaned up a lot of it. There have been copyists working and --
What do they do with that? Are they just in depository?
Well, they're there for students to use.
To use, as a research-reference library.
Right.

Marvelous. Well, why don't we zero in a little bit on your contributions there, and back and forth? Because in a sense, you're paying back, if you want to use that word, to education what you've been really getting from them, and it's a product in dividends, too.
Well, yes, and I think that this past year and the year before, it's reaching a point that I'm most pleased about. If other things went as well, I would be com-

pletely intrigued, and that is simply the fact that this past year, almost 80 percent of all of our dates were in high schools and colleges, and that to me is a very healthy scene. That's where I'd rather be, either as a parttime educator or as just a person who comes to play some music.
Uh-huh.
Either way, I enjoy it very much.
Well, you've been doing clinics and seminars for a long time.
Quite a few years now, but I think -- now we've finally reached the point where it's -- the majority of our time is spent there -- and that's when I'm happiest and I find the bands grooves the most.
I recall you were beginning with that --
In the '70s.
And you --

And something that might also be of interest to people who are not aware that -- I was convinced more by Stan Kenton wanting to convince me to do it than by anyone else. He felt it would be part of my surviving a bad -- not a particularly bad period, but a period that was tough.
Yeah.
And he felt that this would be good therapy for me, plus the fact that it's a much sounder thing than doing things you really don't like to do.
Yes. He talked to you a number of times, didn't he?
Yes, he did.
Have you had very many conferences with people like Stan?

No, the only other -- we used to have periodical meetings, he and I, which was no more than a social thing. But I tried to convince him for a number of years, but he never would go for it, to open a music school out here, and utilize all of our former players who live here, for instance.
Yeah.
And we could offer a curricula that no else was able to. And he always agreed that it was a great idea, but for much later. I kept saying, 'when later?'
Yeah.
And it's unfortunate. I'm sorry we blew it.
Yeah.
Yeah, it would have been a good thing.
I think so. Well, you're doing it your own way now, just right out there. You find that the musicians in the last ten years from the institutions read better?
Oh, yes, there's no comparison.
They can just attack anything,can't they?

That's right, and they're so much better prepared musically. In other words, they're not just walking into a thing of having to learn what they do in a group. They have the music at their fingertips, and they're ready to perform and ready to play, and ready to impress you.
Uh-huh.

And I see some classic examples. They are not all from formal school-type education. A lot of them are from self-taught -- there's still a lot of self-taught players, but they still have a more complete kind of thing going.

In other words, I don't think a young guy could possibly hope to get anywhere, not even to first base, in this day and era, if he didn't have a pretty good knowledge of harmony and structure and all those things that are required now. And if you don't want to go to school, you still have to study with somebody and do a lot of hard work that no one thought too much about in the olden days.
Yeah. Well, that's changed your way of handling the band.

To a great degree, and it certainly changed, I think, the flow of music in this country. I think the tunes and the music in general is far more complex now than it was 15 years ago. And I think it's due to the times and the people and the people involved and the musical educa-
cation system, certainly, to a great extent.
So aside from the technical advances, or preparation that this brings to you, what about the emotional dimension? Does that still -- clear enough? Because each individual has his own --

Yeah, I think it's up to the individual. I've heard a lot of pros and cons about the young players that play very well, but they don't have any feeling. Well, now, that to me is preposterous. You can't play the scale if you don't have feeling. And it's just a question that, once again, many of the people they're listening to perform are players who haven't been heard that much. They don't know their cliches and their stylistic leanings, so they're not overly impressed. And yet, they'll go back to some early player and say, that was it. And I guess -- I know it was, for them. But there were also some people who snuck through that really didn't belong in any period.
Do you find most of the musicians you're getting, the young ones, are familiar with the key historical stylistic approaches of their particular instrument?

Well, I think generally that's becoming more and more important. And evidently it's coming from the right sources, the schools and so on, because I find that for instance, out of the present grouping, there's a -- let's just

pick one instrument, estimate, trumpet. Well, there's -- they can give you on what all the basics on Dizzy and the work structures he was using and so on. But then they are becoming a lot more discerning, and the guy -- they all seem to pay attention to, probably more than anyone, is the young -- who died very young, followed Dizzy, but --
Clifford Brown?
Clifford Brown. There's a big Clifford thing.
Darn right.

In all phases of trumpets. And it goes right down the line this way. The saxophonists, you're going to find alto players that are -- who at one point some years ago would only get as far as Charlie Parker, who are now delving in all directions as to different ways to make your horn sound different, some in a more free kind of aspect than others, and a more governed kind of approach.
So then, even in the activity of your clinics, your musicians in the last decade are enabled to do a better job in helping --

Well, and they're going to be asked questions. The youth now are -- for one thing, there's a good communication line there, because practically every guy in our band, in this current group, for instance, has been in a stage band in a high school at some point in his life.
Uh-huh. Talking to their peers.
That's right.
They went through that same experience.
That's right. And I think that's an important factor in getting a lot of points across and a lot of ideas across.
I think once you told me, maybe within the last year, that there are some people who may be dynamite players, but they don't assume that role of helping others too well, so you don't give a --
No, we don't use them, no.
You just use the people who --
People who can get their job done, that's right. And not every soloist has to be a good clinician.
Sure, yeah.

And I think this is something where the instrument companies and people who set up these things are losing sight. They know if a guy's a great soloist. And he comes in and says, 'Well, how did you do that, sir?' 'Man, I don't know.'
'I just do it.'
Yeah, just do it. Get up here and blow, man.
Uh-huh. Now, I've heard from you about some of the strengths of having these youngsters.
Yeah.
How about the deficits of having these people like this?
I can't really find any heavy deficits.
Good, all right.
And I'll tell you why. For instance, socially and in other ways, this most modern breed are one of the grooviest groups I've ever worked with, as far as just basic people.
Ah-ha.

Which changes a -- everyone can express themselves quite well. We don't have any more of those groupings where they don't even speak to each other, which used to set music back 20 years at a clip. And they're socially conscious, they're out there, and --
You think that's part of --
I think it's part of the --
Generation consciousness and humanistic approach and sensitivity to world problems?
Yeah, they seem to be able to handle an audience and anything else.
I see.

St. John's Cathedral. Located in Milwaukee?

Gregory.

On tenor, yeah.

There's two guys I just want to talk about because they've been with you so long, now. And one is Frank Tiberi. What is it, one decade about now, isn't it?

Ten years, geez. He's contributed an awful lot.

timately.

Well, he's -- I don't think there are too many Frank Tiberians around. If he was a man of his kind, he would be now in Atlantic City, probably the subcontractor at the gaming place or something. But he's not a man of his time, he's a man who still has the spirit to be out here.
Yeah, it's amazing. Yeah. He's writing a book, I understand.
Is he?
Yes, on his own system of improvisational techniques.

Well, I accused him -- many years ago, one of our very first clinician sessions and -- and I walked into a class he was working with, and I came out shaking my head and saying, he's the only person I've ever known in my entire life that sounds like Professor -- what's the guy's name?
Corey?
Corey.
Really?

Absolutely. "And another thing I've been thinking about," and he went into, like, a left field and never came out. All of it.
So that --

Oh, yeah.

Oh, I didn't know that.
Oh, yes, many differet -- [It's why he stays] (unintelligible) in the record business. He sells the records. I have nothing to do with --

Yeah.

Uh-huh.

Yeah, everything. He takes care of transportation, payroll, reservations, --
Right.
-- and very personal things, like --
Calling me for something.
That's right.
Yeah, I know it's always he, and he doesn't forget things, I notice.
No. He's a very complete kind of human being. And I guess you probably have discussed him, I'm sure, with different players in the band at different times. But I've never heard anyone give him a --
Never.
-- a big serious lip about anything.
No, no.
How could you?
No, he's an impartial selfless man.
That's right.
And dedicated, committed to the band and your philosophy.

Well, I think he stands more for the band than he does me, because there's no need to -- like, he knows why I'm there, he knows why the band is there, and he'll above all see first the band gets taken care of and then if there's -- and he will take very good care of me. But the band must be taken care of first.
Uh-huh.
He represents the band.
You are very lucky in having people like that in this day of all kinds of pressures.

Yeah, well, above all I think I was very lucky because I came out of a very trying era in my lifetime, a guy who had been with me for many years who led me into a path of destruction which is still going on, had other people who came up and said, 'We'll try to pull you out of it.' And that's really --
Uh-huh. But he's assumed a lot of those responsibilities, is what you're saying, while he's still on the band as a player.
That's right.
That's remarkable.
To me it is. I think he's a one of a kind by the industry people. And I think you'll get the same answers from agents who sell for Willard Boyd Alexander or anything else.
Is that right? I see.
They respect him. Straight ahead.

Right. Who took over at a very trying time also.
Yeah.
Right about almost the same time that -- well, Bill was stuck with me before that, but Herbie took
over in '68 and --
Oh, it's ten years then. Eleven.
Going on eleven.
And he was in the record distribution business or --

Oh, yeah, since he was a teenager. I knew him when he was a kid (inaudible).
Oh, you did?
Yeah.
Oh, I didn't know that

His parents used to bring him, he and the rest of the family in Connecticut in the (inaudible) late '40s. But I think it's rather -- from an information standpoint, I think it's important to mention the fact that he and -- what the heck was that big
black rock 'n roll drummer in New York in the very early stages of rock, one of his rhythm and blues -- Panama Francis.
Francis?
He and Herbie were both on the same group and did all the rock 'n roll shows.
I had no idea.
It's kind of amazing, because --
Yeah. Well, that's why he's so familiar with the ins and outs of the business.
Well, yeah, he's very close to it, and its part of him.
Yeah, uh-huh.
And I think that our band, which was his earliest influence and bible, wanted to feel like that, except life turned around and he was somewhere else.

Well, you need these kinds of people. Now, most bands that were looking forward to some kind of longevity without people like this, I would find it difficult to see if they could really succeed and keep going.
Yeah, well, I think that's true, but also I think that it's a mutual kind of thing, and a person has to -- I have no control over that part. I went through a very --
Trying --
-- trying period with the person who
started out, as some other people have, being very helpful and all engrossed in my problems and who eventually had his own problems. And I got sucked up in the rest of it.
Yeah, yeah, uh-huh.
And that's unfortunate, but --
Yeah.
-- if you're not keeping your nose close enough to where it's really happening, it can happen to any human being, and it certainly happened to me, and I have no qualms about it, I have no --
No, you're working almost as often as you want to during the course of a year, now, aren't you?
Yes, but it's not really wise.
Yeah, yeah.
I do this for numerous reasons. Number one is, I can't exist without it.
All right.

Number two is to have a halfway decent sounding band, if we were doing it, we almost have to do it this way. But above all, it costs me more money to work than it does not to work, and that's the worst thing that can happen to you.
It does cost you more to work than not to?
Yes.
And so you are working for other purposes?
I'm working for cash flow.
Yeah, I understand.
Nothing more, nothing less.
Uh-huh.
But as far as ever making both ends meet, you never really come close.
I see.
That's why I'm on the phone to lawyers, to tax people, every day of my life.

Yeah.
And you --
I'm sure not everyone's problems could possibly be this weird, but because of my financial connections and what happened a long time ago, this is all aftermath, which has never really stopped.
I see. Is it getting close to being reconciled?
No.
At all?
No.
No?
I'll never live that long. That's when it gets heavy.
Oh, wow.
But also, you become pretty immune to a lot of things. If you have to.
I would think that if it were not for your deep and genuine enthusiasm, commitment, to the music, that this would have driven you off your gourd a long time ago.
Yeah, well, I'm a very stubborn, dumb Polack.
You're just persistent, resilient and all those other things.
Well, I do what I like to do, and I keep doing it because it's my only salvation.

You know, people say -- and this is not anything but almost common knowledge, -- that you're one of the people that -- people don't find you an object of a lot of bad vibes and that kind of thing. But that's just --
(Inaudible.)
Yeah, uh-huh.
But I have certainly been victimized by a lot of other aspects of the business. I've been in trouble
with the Tax Defense Department now for 20 years.
20 years?
There should be a limitation on anything.
Yeah.
Right?

Yeah. Do you think that some of this is responsible for your continuing striving to get the best out of what you do and the guys in the band, all the other connections with the record companies, the radio station or your manager, everyone around you gets caught up in some way with what you would like to do, whether they can match it or not.
Yeah, we all put our best foot forward and hope it comes out, that's all.

Yeah. But I just feel that s highly unusual. Because a lot of people change a lot of parts that you just talked about, like managers, the road manager. But your continuity is very unusual. Look at all the other people who are in the business.

Well, I realize that we all make mistakes and I'm sure that we'll continue to make mistakes. And I try to be a normal -- I hope, just a normal thinking and feeling kind of person. That takes in a lot of --
Territory?
-- territory, but I was raised with a couple of philosophies, and they're very simple ones. You

weren't put on this earth to have a ball, is number one. And number two is, it's not important to amass a fortune, because what you never had, you'll never miss. These are the chief philosophies, and they work.
You've had those as lifelong things.
Yeah.

Uh-huh, good. You want to say something about your family now? You have your grandchildren and so forth. I think that ought to be something for the record here. You have one daughter. How old is she now?
She was born in '42. And my -- our grandson is going to be 19 in March.
Tommy.
Tom, and Alexandra is 17. And --
Wow.
Yes, a lot has happened.
Right.

What's the name of the group?
I don't know. It's young people who have been involved in the country and bluegrass singing for quite
awhile. But they have a crossover job which is involved (inaudible) with the pop-rock aspect of it.
What does Tommy -- does he play in that?
Yeah, he plays guitar and sings and they're playing some of his songs.
Uh-huh.

Inge is -- right, she's a bluegrass fiddle player (inaudible). And still makes most of her living from that.
And they've been making their home in Nashville for how many years?
Several years now. Eight seven, eight, nine years.
They used to live --
In San Francisco.
-- in the San Francisco area. Well, let's see.
(Recording interrupted.)

there's interest in to what degree you are the boss of the band. Well, I think the best way to describe my position, it's the same one I started with a long time ago. I'm the coach. I really honestly sincerely believe I'm the best coach that there is in the entire music business. Anymore than Woody Hayes would think he was the best coach in college football or the late -- who was the great coach from Green Bay whom I had such respect for?
I know who you're saying.
Italian name. Whatever his name was, I once received --
It starts with L, Lombardi?
Vince Lombardi. The highest compliment I ever received in my entire life was from a nightclub operator in Buffalo, New York, a real dese and dem and dose guy.
Yeah?

And he still tended bar in his own club so you knew he was a downhome cat. And I came off the bandstand and the place had a tin roof and it sounded terrible. And he was in a trance, and he said, "Wood, that's the best band I ever heard in my life. Man, too much." He said, "You da Vince Lombardi of the bands."

And that to me was the epitome of everything that anyone could say. The second-best compliment I ever received in my life was just this past year, when the bus pulled up to a truck stop, and to let the guys out to get whatever they needed, a hamburger or whatever --
Where was this?

I believe in Illinois somewhere. It doesn't really matter. The locale is not really the important thing. And right across the road, on the other side, there was a truck stop on one side, where most of the guys-- in fact, all of them went in here. But right across the road was a McDonald's, and I had never really been in a McDonald's, and I thought, 'Well, now's the time to case a McDonald's, and I'll try their hamburger.'

And I went in and I was waiting on line to get my hamburger. And a little girl about 13 or 14 was the cleanup girl. She got a little broom and a little thing and picks up dirty paper dishes and so on. And she came over and she gave me a very strange look and then she went over and did a little more, and then she came back and watched out of the corner of her eye, with a funky little attitude.

And I finally looked around, and she came over very close and she said, 'Are you Woody Herman?' And I said, 'Yeah.' And she said, 'Wow,' and split. That was the second-highest compliment I ever received in my life.
Oh, that's beautiful. Yeah, that says a lot.
It does to me.
Yeah, yeah, both have different dimensions of your total --
Exactly. But it was important to me to realize -- I'm sure that this little kid had been at a high school concert of a high school thing. But she was just stating her case. She was gassed.
Yeah, good, good.
Beautiful feeling.
Well, I have this question, I don't know if you want to show your style a bit. When you're not on this earth, what's going to happen to all this stuff?

I don't have too much faith that anything will happen. Of course, I made some very strong statements years ago when I was in the prime of my attitudes, when I said, that if I found another Herd roaming the earth I would come back to life to extinguish it. But I don't feel that badly about it anymore. You do have to become a lot more philosophical and if there was a dollar to be made for the benefit of anyone I'd go ahead and continue. But that's the only reasons.
I see, I see.
I have no long range plans.
Yeah, you haven't even contemplated about apparent heirs to the music leadership or anything.
No. No, I would prefer if one of my family wanted to do something about it. But no big plans, because I don't think it's worth it, planning.
Yeah, uh-huh. Well, I'm sure that's crossed many peoples' minds, all those bands, I'm sure.
Well, --
People who have become institutions in the bands.
Oh, yeah, but I have no feeling for that nostalgic efforts and all that.
Yeah.
And so if I thought it could be beneficial to my grandson, let's say, we'll say, then go ahead and do it. But I would hope that he would present whatever he liked.
Uh-huh. Right, right, I understand what you're saying. That would be in the spirit of your own philosophy.
That's right, exactly, straight ahead. Don't worry about what went down, because you won't be able to emulate it even if you wanted to.
Of course, ridiculous.
I don't care about all that. That's self adulation. I don't dig it.
Good, okay. Has all this been worth it to you now? Obviously, -- I don't know whether there was a point of no return, but I don't think that's necessarily true for everybody.
No, I don't think --

We were talking about whether this whole long safari of yours in jazz, big bands, the whole music industry, has been worth it to you.

Uh-huh. What have been the key attributes that make you feel that way, that it's worth doing it all over again?

Well, I think it's the music itself. I think that's the most valuable and most important factor. There's a lot of things you have to give away, such as comfort and relaxation, and to a great extent -- but there are things that I think more than make up for it, too, in the fact that you receive a great amount of stimulation from the music and from people, from audiences, and from the travel to every corner of the earth.
Uh-huh.
