Well, naturally, we're always looking
for some sort of Utopia, some sort of more suitable path. And I think the one dominant factor that makes it as difficult as it is is the travel.
Uh-huh.

And travel in itself is not all that bad in this day and age, but the length of jumps, the amount of mileage that is still an imperative and important factor, and I don't feel that the people who direct and set up tours and book them really take enough consideration of what the human mind and body will stand.
I see. Well, if it's impractical, your manager Hermie screens some of those out.

Oh, you do, of course. But after all, the most important situation, I think, above all is that you earn enough to take care of your expenses. And there are too many weeks, still, where we are not able to really even break even. And consequently, the many weeks where you do make a profit, the profit is gone for the bad weeks.
And this makes it really -- in that department, it's really a very difficult balancing act that one has to perform.
Now, was this true in the '40s as well as in the '70s, now, closing this decade?
Well, probably, but it wasn't as evident because in the first place, we were -- during much of that time we were in wartime, and you couldn't do the amount of travel
that the agencies and booking people would probably want you or like for you to do.
Uh-huh.
We were limited, and so it made our life, -- even though it was still rough, it made it somewhat better than it is even today.
Yeah, I was wondering about that.

We had more one-week places to play, places like theatres. And even though they were very hard also on the nervous system because of the preposterous schedules, five and six and seven shows a day, without a day open, and you would close one theatre after a last show at, say, 11:30 or midnight, and then catch a train, either very early in the morning or right after the theatre, and travel on to the next town and open the following morning.
Boy.
So it was another -- but even that was somewhat more comfortable, I guess, than doing one nighters all year round and having to travel every day of your life.
Well, that's hard to foresee, what changes might appear in the future for people who want to continue with bands.
Yeah, well, there are more and more new people involved in the band -- big band field today, but I don't feel that they're really being realistic about it, because in
They're feel we're losing the chance to be a part of something that they will never be able to do in any other kind of music, or get done in small groups.

What you mention brings to mind a comment that was made by young Richie Cole, the alto player. And reflecting about his experience with Buddy Rich's band, he said, 'You know, a big band experience is like a period piece.' That was very good, because it's there, and if you don't pick it up, it's gone.

That's right, and you may never have that opportunity. Because, the fact, as I've always truly thought, that a group that stays together, even for a matter of months, and works every night, is a much better group than one that stays together five years and meets once or twice a week.
Uh-huh, I see what you're saying.
There's no doubt about it.
Do you have any feelings about why this problem is the way it is now?

I really don't. I do know, though, just by looking around us at the high school level, and I find that the majority of players, no matter what part of the country it is, and the kids that are really enthusiastic about it, are the white kids. And I don't know the reason. Maybe they become more enthusiastic because they're into the feeling of the big band sound, I'm not sure.

But I think a great deal of that is, I think, is, the motivation is caused and made possible by the teaching staff, the people that are involved in the teaching. And maybe there aren't enough black teachers to begin with.

Yeah. I was at a NAGE executive board meeting a couple of weeks ago, and several members of the Association's advisory council are black and they showed up, and echoed something that I had heard in the last couple of years, that even the Jazz Education Association isn't able to dispel this feeling that you have big bands in jazz education and that's what it's about, and that we ought to emphasize the other by virtue of placing emphasis more on improvisation. It might happen. That's what the blacks were saying.
Yeah.
And they were deploring the fact, too.

Well, then, too, I don't think there's been a great deal of enthusiasm displayed by the two black bands that are successful, reasonably successful, in this country, in -- I've not ever known Basie to hold a seminar or do any of the things that some of us have been doing for quite a few years.
That's true.
And I don't hear much about the Ellington band being involved in it. So, now, whether it's their reasoning that for some purpose or nonpurpose that this
most cases they are basically glorified rehearsal bands, and -- who on occasion play some engagements.
Well, that's kind of a commentary, too, of what I just heard, that Thad and Mel's band is breaking up. I don't know if you knew that.

Well, I don't know if it was ever really organized. So that's really being candid, because for several years it was a Monday night band in New York City. Every Monday night they met and played the music. And then in more recent times, they've gone to different parts of the world, and tried to -- I renamed them the Bed and Board Band, and only for the reason that they were accepting engagements just to have a band. That was their only purpose. And it's a very wonderful purpose except that I don't feel that it's righteous in a business and in a career or in a profession, as it supposedly is sometimes termed, to not be able to sustain yourself with an income of some kind of regularity.
I see.

And it was because these two guys loved what they were doing so much that they put up with almost anything and everything, things that I think were really preposterous, in relation to the effort they were putting into it and the young people they eventually wound up with. Because some time ago, they lost most of the they took more mature players who live in New York and played with them on Monday nights.
Uh-huh.
The minute you went through Lincoln Tunnel, that was the end of that band, in most instances.

Yeah, I noticed that the last year or two they've had some problems with personnel, and then Thad had mentioned something. I just wondered what you thought about this as a perspective or a part of the perspective for the big band business and schools.

He's had an extremely difficult time, as he says, in motivating young black players to go on the road with a big band. They just wanted to say, 'Well, I want to be a star and lead a small group, because that's where it is,' and that was part of their agenda, to make sure it was that way between the two of them.
Yeah.
And that might have been part of the ongoing problem.

It could very well be, because if you've noticed in our case, in the last few years, it's just less and less black people that go through our band. And it's tougher and tougher to find one who really wants to be a member of our band or any band.
I see.
And I don't know what motivates them in that direction. But whatever it is, it's too bad, because I
happens this way, I'm certainly not aware and I'm not trying to do a critique, either.
Yes.
It's just that I don't understand why they aren't doing it. I know Basie appears at many schools, but only in a two-hour concert and it has nothing to do with --
Anything else.
Anything else.
That's a good observation. Well, so that doesn't seem to be much hope in the horizon to correct it.
Well, I can't think of anything right offhand, but I think that if concentrated effort were put into it by any grouping, that it could go nowhere but up, because you're starting from scratch, really.

Well, maybe Thad and Mel's band was trying to, since it was integrated and they were working on it. Although, I heard some things also about the quality of the clinics there, that there weren't too many small-group seminars, like you do, with the sections and so forth. It was all, like, well, what we have to say is for the whole group, and they'd just do it and say, well, that's their seminar.
Well, it's kind of difficult.
Well, we'll see. I have some things I was reviewing, the other ones that we kind of missed out on, to pick up on.
All right.
There were some people that I was interested in having either more comments or comments about. One we left out completely was Jim Pugh. What about Jim?
Well, Jim Pugh as I think we've all learned has become one of the truly outstanding jazz musicians anywhere, in this day and age.

He made two entrances into our band. The first time he came as a second trombonist to Bobby Burgess, and we weren't -- I for one and I think several other people in the band were not overly enthusiastic about Jim's playing. We thought he was more than adequate, but not truly anyone that we felt was going to be showing any brilliance.
Uh-huh.

And yet, when Burgess decided to leave, we felt that Jim would be worth a try on lead. And this evidently was the move that he needed and it turned out to be utterly fantastic. His rise was that of a meteor, in other words, it seemed like overnight he just started to grow and leaps and bounds as far as his abilities on the trombone.
You thought he was a find of the last 25 years.
I would say that within the last 25 or 30 years he was one of the truly outstanding talents that went through the Herd.
Wow, regardless of what instrument.
That's right.
When was that, that Bobby left?
It would be in the early '70s.
Yeah. But Jim he stayed with you quite awhile.
Once he settled in, yes. As a matter of fact, he it was with me the better part of -- well, over four years, actually.
What kind of influence did he have on, say, the young bone players that were coming in and out of the band? I know he was --

Oh, I think he was very important and whenever it was possible we would utilize players from Eastman where he had studied, because they would have the same approach, general approach, to the way to play it and blow a trombone.
What was that, briefly? What was different about the Eastman graduate?

Well, there was a particular trombone teacher there, and I can't give you his name right offhand, but his approach evidently was that which made people not play extremely forceful. It was a different approach, and it's gone on through now, after Pugh, Pew, on into the young man whom I find to be a most likely replacement for Jimmy Pugh, and that is Birch Johnson. And I think his future also is one of tremendous possibilities.
And then he became a marvellous soloist.
Yes, it happened in both cases.
Was Byrgh also that way when he came in?
Yeah, exactly.
Amazing, isn't it?

It's some kind of a -- it's almost like a charm, with that particular school, as far as brass players are concerned. It holds true of some of the trumpet players I had go through the band from there. I'll pick one at random. Alan Vizzutti, who I think is one of the outstanding sheer legitimate trumpet players that I've ever heard in my entire life.
And both of them, that is, Jim and Al, are with Chick Corea now.
On and off they are, yeah. As a matter of fact, I think that, for your edification and mine, that Alan Vizzutti will be at the Great American Music Hall tonight.
No kidding.
Yeah.
That's fantastic. Is he taking someone else's place or --
Yes, because we have a new man coming in and I would prefer to have someone with us that knew the book and so on.
Well, that's fantastic. Where is he living
now? Down South or --
Los Angeles.
Oh, good. That'll be wonderful.
And very busy, as we would all expect.
I neglected to mention, this is January 21, 1979 today. The Super Bowl day. How about -- you have had both Jim and Burch playing things that are legato oriented, ballads and things --
Ballad-style, yeah, it's a jazz --
Yeah, yeah. And you've also had some marvelous players in the past that did a job that you would rank as very, very high. Urbie Herbie Green.
Oh, yeah.
And --
And as a matter of fact, I've had probably one of the best arrays of trombone players of anyone who ever had a band. It started with Bill Harris and --
And Earl Swope.

Yeah, Earl Swope for awhile, and then there was Carl Fantana later, and along with people like Urbie Herbie Green, we had later -- I'm trying to think of the fellow from New Orleans who was orginally with the Al Belletto group. Another marvelous trombonist, Jimmy -- I cannot think of his last name.
I can't either. I'll have to check that.
But Another marvellous trombonist and then at different times for very short periods, we had people come through the band like Kai Winding and people like that.
Oh, that's right. Frank Rehak.
Frank Rehak, yes, of course, and several others.

Yeah, you've been very fortunate. I notice, too, whether this is valid or not, but in judging a lot of jazz festivals the last three years, I think it's rather clear there's a dearth of fine trombone players.
Yeah, that's true, yeah.
They're very hard to find.
Yeah.
There just aren't that many in the schools.
Yeah, that's true, but there are the exceptions, and when they are, they're really something else.
While we're at that, there's something I want to quote to you and see what you think because I thought about you when I read this.
This is a couple of years ago, a year and a half ago, but this is an interview with Phil Woods. And he had something to say about the schools, and I wanted to read this to you, if I may.
All right.
June, 1977, and Phil the fellow says, 'Now,

every college and school has a jazz band, and I have a great fear that we're going to turn out jazz teachers instead of jazz players. It's self proliferating. Cats get their degree, there are no gigs, so they go back to school and teach other kids how not to get a gig. Jazz is in danger of being isolated at the academy.

"Now, I did go to Juillard but it wasn't a cocoon. These other places are too sanitary. The very word clinic makes me cringe, when they ask, 'Are you going to give a clinic,' I say, 'Yes, send in the patients.' My idea of a great course is this: After I got a band together, I'd hire a bus, then everybody would pack their bags, get on the bus and just drive around the campus for eight or ten hours. Then have the cats set up, tune up, put on their uniforms, but they don't play their horns. Then back on the bus for eight hours.
"This has nothing to do with music. It's called reality." He's trying to --
I find it very amusing, and that is sad. I hope that we never get to that stage.
No.

And the one thing he's forgetting about completely is that there are really many, many exceptional young players who do develop. And if there isn't a gig, they will make a gig, which was really the way it started. And it's really the way Mr. Woods started, and he was a very good educa-
tor, and he was one of the first people to be involved at the high school level, of teaching kids at that age.
That's true.
And I think what he's saying, probably, he's happier doing what he's doing today, and I'm sure he is.
Yeah.
But that has nothing to do with the real reality.
Yeah, okay. I thought it was funny.
Truly.
That's how he is. I like his humor. He's a very sharp guy.

Anyway, now, let's see, I had another gentleman I wanted more on. Yeah, could you speak more about Sal Nestico, a little more about him? How he got in your band, for instance. I don't think we had that. How did he come to your band?
Well, through our upstate contigent, upstate New York. I had heard about his playing prior to joining us, his playing with the Mangione Brothers, they had a group called the Jazz Brothers.
Right.

And I never heard too much conversation about the Mangione Brothers, but I sure heard a lot of talk about -- wherever the group appeared, whether it be Buffalo or Utica or any of those upstate New York places, about this tenor
player who was supposed to be a real whirlwind. And he really came in as a sub into our band, I think. Nat Pierce found him somewhere, and he was trying to get located around New York, I guess.
I see.
And he really started with us, just prior to the time we went into the Metropole.
Uh-huh.
And I think it gave a the great amount of people, the first shot at hearing a whole new kind of player, at least for the age we were living in then, --
Yeah.

And as far as sheer excitement and sheer joy of playing, I don't think I ever met anyone who could surpass Sal. Unfortunately, and once again, I'm only bringing up these points because I feel they had something to do with his true -- lack of true success, and I feel that one of his hindrances was the fact that he was one of those kind of great soloists who maybe should have studied a little bit. And I'm not certainly talking about lack of knowledge of music itself, but there's a -- with the playing of any instrument, there is generally an air of legitimacy that keeps you in -- constantly in the swim of things.
And if he had developed, -- not because I wanted him to do it, but if he had developed a kind of rapport with the
studio scene --
Oh, I see.

-- I feel that he would have been able to become much more than he did. Because there was still -- we had him doing many things in the band, because we had this great feeling and understanding of the man's ability and his great native ability and his great feeling.
But -- as a matter of fact, Nat Pierce, because he wanted to help in the development of Mr. Nastico, wrote a ballad for him one time on "Easy Living."
"Easy Living."

Which later turned out to be played by every tenor player that went through the band. And he played it very well. But there were certain -- just simple flaws that make the difference, like intonation on intervals and things of that nature, where all his concentration had been on swinging and making the changes right, and Mr. Time himself and all that sort of thing.
But the little --
Nuances.
Yeah, the little things that make the difference were always missing.
I see.
And even all the time he spent in Europe, where most guys who go to Europe and want to continue to eat and
sleep wind up in one radio band or another somewhere, in Germany or -- somehow. And then they will try to get playing gigs on the side so they don't lose their mind completely.

But Sal was able to sustain himself some sort of way in Europe for several years, and never have to play in a studio band, so he didn't. And he beat the rap, except that had he played in one of those bands, he probably would have developed in many other lines. I just had the feeling that he was not the kind of human that you could really put harnesses on or chains, probably a better way to try to describe it would be to say, to shackle with discipline.
Oh, okay, that's a good --
And he was just not that kind of person in every way.

I just heard an album about a month ago, that was put together by some German. And Mike Baron that Sal was playing -- it was a big band, I don't know what it's all about, there wasn't much background on it. But it was while he was over there.
Uh-huh.
Or whether he was just in and out or whether --
I don't know.
Yeah. Well, that's --
It was Mike Baron's band?
And a German.
I see.
Yeah, interesting.
It might have been like a workshop band or it might been a working group.
Yeah, yeah. It was this British player, Alan Skidmore, that was playing, a saxophone player. Yeah, I think that Sal was a pretty prominent figure in the annals of the Herds.
Oh, definitely, yeah.
In his work, and he kind of set a model for many players, maybe in the band's mind, too, that, 'Boy, we need a swinger like that.'
That's right, that -- and carry the ball at any speed.
Uh-huh, because Gregory did a magnificent job in carrying many of those kinds of responsibilities, but he had more.
Yeah, it was his other facets that were really more important, I thought, his ballad facets and doubles and so on.
Let's see. How about Serge Chaloff? I know we're going back to these key figures.
Well, I think he was one of the earlier swinging jazz baritone saxophonists. A very loose and free
spirit in every direction, and that kind of player. He was heavily influenced by the early bop music, and he played baritone somewhat like Charlie Parker played alto. It was that --
Are there other outstanding baritone players in your band? I know you had Tommy Anastasis and Frank Hipner and people like that.
Yeah, Hipner was a very -- truly outstanding jazz player, but he was a kind of a strange young man, and he still resides, I think, in Reno.
Oh, does he?
Yeah.
I haven't heard about him for a long time.
And he works in a restaurant or something.
Really?
Yeah.
Oh, I thought he was a complement to the band.
Oh, yes, great player and I've had some really excellent baritone saxophonists in recent years, too.
Bruce Johnson.
Bruce Johnson, I think, is truly outstanding, and then currently I have a young man that I think is -- touches a brilliancy.
Oh, yes? What's his name?
His name is Gary Semolian.
Oh, yes.
And he's from Long Island area, actually, or Westchester. Several other players are from that place, and played in different school bands and different road-shop workshop bands in that area.
Uh-huh. I was thinking about something when you said upstate New York and so forth --
And then, of course, there was a baritone -- excuse me, again, for jumping around, but I get flashbacks in memory.
Sure, go ahead.
There's a baritone saxophonists that I think is one of the real giants in the last 15 years or more, and who's a contemporary of, once again, that area of upstate New York, northern New York.
Yeah.
Oh, I'm going to have trouble with names again. But he's just excellent, an Italian name. Brignola.
Nick Magnola.
That's it. He's fabulous.
You want to say some things about him?
Well, I just feel that as a sheer, stampin', stop-and swinging baritone saxophonist, it's pretty hard to beat this guy.
I would say so.
Yeah.
On the contemporary scene today, I don't know of anyone who plays like him.
Not quite like he does.
Yeah. Well, that's good to hear.
And some of the people that had been established for years are very good, but they are -- there's not that kind of spirit to them.
That's the word. Yeah, that kind of spirit is kind that Sal had, too, wasn't it?
Yeah, exactly.
You're talking about that kind of verve.
Yeah, right.
Nick has been recording a few things.
Yes, I understand that.
Finally.
Which I'm very pleased about.
That's good to hear.
I -- it's interesting that Jerry Mulligan is putting together a band, or attempting to, under the aegis of Mr. Willett and Alexander.
Large? Small?
I guess it's a pretty big band, 12 or 14.
Oh, really?
Yeah. And he's doing a lot of the old music.
Concert Jazz Band stuff.
Yeah, that stuff, and even some of the earlier --
Oh, I see.
-- tentet stuff and so on.
Uh-huh.

And he played a festival with us in Germany, I guess, two or three years ago. And once again, I hope that I'm making myself clear, but I feel that his absence from the scene has not helped him as a player.
Correct. I believe that, too.
Yeah.
I just heard him on a Michel Legrand album, soloing. It was good to hear him.
Sure.
Wonderful to have him back. Yeah, Nick -- I hope something will move with Nick, because he's a rarity.
Right. And he's in a education.
Right. Now, when was he in your band? He was in it just a short time, wasn't he?
Yeah, just a few months.
Yeah.
In the '60s.
Yeah, he mentioned that to me once.
Yeah, yeah.
When he was with Tim Curzon's band. Yeah, you seem to have drawn from certain -- either cluster of schools or geographical sections.
Yeah, I don't know why that --
Yeah, it happens, doesn't it?
But our system, which is purely the system of having letting the players decide who comes in the band makes this happen.
When there's a natural process.
That's right. And once again, we're having some changes, and it's pretty much up to the people that are going to have to play with them.
Oh, I see. So --
In other words, if we need a trumpet player, we talk to the trumpet section.
"Who do you know? Who do you recommend?"
That's right. And same with trombones and the same with the saxophones.
And this then determines the network of kind of little chain reactions.
Yeah, mostly, in the long run. And then, of course, once in a while, somewhere out of the dim blue you'll hear from one of the people on the teaching staff at Berkeley
or --
Yes.
-- North Texas or anywhere. They'll say, 'Hey, I've got a kid here who I just think is going to be something else.'
I see.
And then we very often have taken a shot that way, and very often it works out. It's not too often we have to (inaudible) [pick] on somebody.
I know that during the upstate New York focus, did you have Joe Romano, too? Wasn't he --
Oh, sure.
Yeah. He had a certain amount of drive.
Joe first joined us in California. He was -- I don't know what he was doing out there. He was there, and we made some changes overnight and he was one of them and Bill Perkins was the other.
Oh, I see.
They came in the band at the same time.
Oh.
There were a lot of interesting players in the band, during that period.
You sure have, yeah. I bet you can take every section and then start putting names down on that heading and then see --
See how many --

See who you would come up with. That's really incredible. Yeah, I was interested in that because I knew I would prompt you to think about how the band gets its recruits and replacements and the adaptations of these new recruits.
Now, Bill Berne has a key role in helping to facilitate --

Oh, absolutely. Without his stick-to-itiveness we would probably never be able to make any changes, because the geography and the hassles of transportation and making everything dovetail, it's just beyond human endeavor and yet he seems to accomplish it 99 percent of the time.

I'll ask you what kind of a grass roots problem, about when people come in, because I've heard people around me sometimes, when you're playing. And they'll say, 'Oh, there's another new guy over there. Now, how do they outfit these young guys with the clothes?' Now that...
Pretty badly.
I'm just wondering, they come in and --
Well, in the back of the bus, we have a whole bunch of fitting rooms where nobody gets fitted, ever.
Uh-huh.
But Bill has this thing -- and that's why he hates to change uniforms, no matter how threadbare they
are, because then the real work sets in for him. Where you have 15 players, you maybe have to have 30 uniforms. We have a variety of --
Sizes.
-- usuals and then you have a few extra large and then you have a few midget sizes for the smaller men.
Do they turn in their jackets, like people turn in their uniforms when they leave the service?
They can't wait, they'd like to burn them but (inaudible).
(laughter)
Do they really do that?
Yeah, they leave the uniforms. It's not really a personal thing. It's just -- you wear -- a football player, there's a number on his back.
Yeah, okay.
We never talked about that, and I thought that might be --

Yeah, it's pretty amusing. And it's saddening, too, because -- particularly my wife gets so hacked about this, because very often we have a finelooking group of young people, and she says, 'It's such a drag to look at them, they're not really well dressed, instead of those things.' And I say, well, --
Well, the Lawrence Welk band.
They have a suit for each occasion, all bad.
Yeah. Well, I know that's a practical thing with changes.
Right.
It's another job that Bill has, then.
Exactly. All the jobs that no one really ever would want. Bill takes them on with complete assurance and gets it done.
Are there other things like that, other than uniforms?

Oh, my God, there's so many things he takes care of. Payroll, he takes care of -- and there are constant personal problems with people, and he gets it all. I don't. It's got to be really drastic before somebody hits on me for whatever it is, after they've been through the whole thing.
Yeah.
And I will, after I've known a person for a long time, offer some little advice, but very -- really, I try to stay out of peoples' personal lives and --
Unless they may come to you.
That's right.
Seek counsel.
But Bill really has to be confessor,
everything.
I see. Well, he probably would be a good one to talk to someday. He must have a million things.
He would. Definitely.

As a matter of fact, one of the things I wanted to talk with you a little later on, is dealing with the road, but I'll hold that for a minute or two. Sonny Berman was a young player that we didn't discuss.

Yeah. I think he was truly outstanding for his period in his very short lifetime. When he did some of his greatest playing with the band, he was 21, and I guess he died shortly -- during that same year. So actually, he probably started with us when he was 19 and wound up when he was 21.
Do you recall how he got on, a guy like that?
I really don't know.
Out of high school, practically.

Yeah, but he'd been around New York and he was building a little reputation among the younger players. And people like Neal Hefty and a couple of the other trumpet players knew of him and said that they thought he'd be fine.
And he certainly did work out, beautifully. I heard more of Sonny's playing the other night. I dug up some bootleg album that had quite a period of things, probably taken from
broadcasts, I'm not sure. They're not overly well recorded. And some of them were right off the line of a radio commercial we were doing. The Old Gold Show.
Old Gold Show.
But it's probably more Berman than I've heard, ever.
Really?
Didn't realize -- every little pop tune he had eight bars or 16 bars, and everything he did was extremely interesting, not just any run-of-the-mill eight bars, you know.
Uh-huh.
Yeah, really amazing.
He had a very mature concept.
Yes, really.
The few things that were really commercially documenting his work.
Right.
So he's kind of been an ongoing figure of the First Herd.
That's right.
So I was just curious about it.

He was one of the highlights, I think, of that band. Pete Condoli was in that band, with Sonny at the same time. And later Conte, a couple of years later. And, of course, the lead trumpet player was very good. From Connecticut. Turn it off for a second and I'll try to come up with it.
Okay.
(Recording interrupted.)
Before the war?

Yeah, very early in the war, he was the lead trumpet player with Claude Thornhill's band which was a very musical and very beautiful band. And then I think during part of that war period, I believe he was with the Artie Shaw band, in the Navy. Then when he got out, he joined me. Oh, God -- Conrad Gazzo.
Oh, Conrad.
Yeah.
Yeah, the Italian.
And this was one of the great trumpet -- I think each individual was a complete individual and made a fantastic section.
Okay. You know, Pete's been playing a lot of hotels and shows and -- did he recruit his brother for you?

Well, his brother came to visit during the summer or something to hang out with his older brother. And we were at that point using four trumpets, so I said, 'How's he play?' And Pete says, 'He's coming along pretty good.' So I said, 'Well, give him a chair and a stand,' and had Ralph scribble out some -- doubling the lead parts or something.
Let him play, eh?
So that's how that started, and then when
the following season he got out of school, we put him in the band.
I see. So he was that promising, from what you heard.
Yeah.
Pete -- well, he was called Superman. Why was that?

Well, he did a Superman tune, a number with us, and at theatres. It originally started out as a gag and it turned out to be quite a thing. And for instance, the Paramount Theatre he flew down on a wire from a very high balcony down to the stage.
He did?
And he came -- would land and go right into the bridge of 'Apple Honey', (inaudible), yeah. (Singing.)
Is that right?
Yeah.
Did he have a Superman suit and the whole --
