And I recorded a couple of very, very old songs with a legendary figure down in Nashville by the name of Mac Wiseman, who's a very strong influence and has been for many years in the bluegrass field.
How do you spell his name?
W-i-s-e-m-a-n.
Oh, that one.
And Mac, M-a-c-.
Yeah.
And we did an old tune that was first introduced a hundred years ago by Gene Austin, called My Blue Heaven. // //
Oh, yeah.
And then we took an old tune that you will remember because it was done a lot by jazz people. // If I Could Be With You One Hour Tonight. // And found out that Harry
Barris
Berenson in the late '20s, wrote a song to be sung or played as an obligato against that tune, called It Must Be True.
Really.

And so we did the oldest gimmick in the world, (inaudible) which is, the last half of the last chorus. One sings one tune and the other sings the other tune. And we had what they call in Nashville circles housewives' disco beat. Which Threw me a curve.
Was this some singles or some --
Yeah, just -- we did this as a single recording, which should be out any time. I'm waiting for the final mix. The producer is a very consistent guy down there who's had much success.
What's the label?
I don't know my friend's label. I have to find out, but it's -- but he's had some pretty good showing on the charts in the country field.
And so it'll be Herman and Wiseman or Wiseman and Herman or something like that.
It's not Tommy Martin's --
Yeah, it's his label, yeah.
It is his label.
Yeah.
Well, I'll be darned.
Yeah.
You try everything.

Well, sure, why not? I've recorded with Bing, I've recorded with Nat Cole, we sang together. I recorded with Dinah Shore. This was all many, many years ago. And then I've done everything from every kind of country tune to every kind of honkytonk blues tune. And so --
Why not?
I enjoyed it. It was fun.
So you didn't play on this. You just sang.
No, just sang.
What kind of group was behind you? A bluegrass group?
No, it was just a regular, typical session, Nashville type players.
Oh, I see, yeah.
And they used the same rhythm sound basically, except that they're doing their theme. thing.
I see.

But they used the base drum without the lot to front on it, and the whole thing -- the same as a rock thing. And the piano player was fantastically good in his world. And two good guitar players and a base player, and they work out their charts. And then you sing to them.
I see.
That's the way it's done in Nashville.
I see. Well, good. That brings us up to
That's it.
Okay. Thank you, Woody.
Right.
I really appreciate it.
This is Herb Wong, concluding an interview with Woody Herman, in Berkeley, California, on January 21, 1979.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Copyright notice, interview introduction and recent road tour
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright notices, Smithsonian header and Herb Wong's introduction. Herman describes the band's recent Florida, Carolinas, Virginia and New York dates.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Singing and dancing in a children's movie prologue at age nine
segments.summary: Herman says his father steered him toward theatre; he did his first tour at nine singing and dancing in a kid unit doing a prologue to the film School Days, and used the money to buy a saxophone.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Milwaukee teachers and growing bored with show business
segments.summary: After getting the saxophone and clarinet he studied with local teachers, and by high school was tired of the song-and-dance act.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: First jazz records: Red Nichols, Indiana Five, Ellington's Washingtonians
segments.summary: In his freshman year of high school early jazz records drew him in, including Red Nichols and Duke Ellington's eight-piece group that sounded like jungle music.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Birth date, records and radio at home
segments.summary: Born May 16, 1913, in Milwaukee. He bought his own records and listened to dance bands on an Atwater Kent radio in his room.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Parochial school bands and private teachers Buech, Kruger and Rudy Wiedoeft
segments.summary: His school had little music program, so he studied privately with Arthur Buech, Arthur Kruger and Walker, plus a couple of lessons with Rudy Wiedoeft.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Parents' doubts about a musician's career and music in the household
segments.summary: His parents lost enthusiasm when he chose to be a musician rather than a performer, until he became a bandleader. His father had good taste and a player-piano with classical rolls.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: MCA band brochures and deciding on a career in bands
segments.summary: As a grade-school kid he collected MCA brochures of uniformed bands and decided that was what he wanted to do.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Early player influences: Goodman, Bigard, Trumbauer, Teagarden, Miff Mole
segments.summary: From Red Nichols records and Ellington he heard Benny Goodman, Barney Bigard, Frank Trumbauer and Jack Teagarden, whose assurance impressed him; he was not impressed by Miff Mole.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: House band at the Eagles Ballroom in Milwaukee
segments.summary: In high school he played tenor and clarinet in the ballroom house band five nights a week, meeting visiting bands like Paul Whiteman's.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Leader Joe Lichter, learning to read and helping each other
segments.summary: Singing came from vaudeville. Joe Lichter led the band; older saxophonists helped Herman, a poor reader, and he comments on camaraderie among players.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Tom Garen's band: music as business, Ginny Simms and Tony Martin
segments.summary: He left Milwaukee for Tom Garen's San Francisco band, which taught him music as a business and entertainment; Ginny Simms and Tony Martin were in it.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early bands
segments.title: Harry Sosnick, joining Isham Jones and the Isham Jones Juniors
segments.summary: After about two and a half years with Garen he joined Harry Sosnick's radio band, then Isham Jones, where he made his first musical recordings and led the Juniors small group.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Forming a cooperative band after Isham Jones retired in 1936
segments.summary: When Jones retired, five members set up a stockholder corporation modelled on Bob Crosby's band. It ran as a cooperative for eight or nine years before dissolving.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Playing alto and hiring Ellington sidemen for record dates
segments.summary: He began playing alto in the section, and used Johnny Hodges, Ben Webster and Juan Tizol on record dates when Ellington's men were restless.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Decca contract, Roseland and the Famous Door: struggling to survive
segments.summary: The band was nearly a Decca house band, covering hits, and survived the early lean years at Roseland, on the road and at the Famous Door.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Early sidemen and arrangers: Bishop, Jenkins, Noble, Harper
segments.summary: He names the first band's rhythm section, Joe Bishop's writing, and outside arrangers Gordon Jenkins, James Noble and Nick Harper.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Dave Kapp at Decca: blues and folk repertoire, then Frenesi
segments.summary: Dave Kapp gave him a free hand with folk and blues records like the Blues on Parade series, yet also pushed him to sing Frenesi.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Wood-chopper's Ball and Decca's patient re-release system
segments.summary: Decca re-released records that had not caught on, which is how Woodchopper's Ball became a hit; some early Ralph Burns arrangements were also done there.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Leaving Decca for Columbia after comparing studio sound
segments.summary: The Decca studio sound bothered him, so he made V-discs at Columbia and RCA before choosing Columbia on sound alone.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Radio airtime and losing money at hotels
segments.summary: The band was on Mutual radio from Roseland, and airtime later justified losing money at New York hotels to earn it back on the road.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Women instrumentalists and new colors: vibes, guitar, Ralph Burns
segments.summary: He hired trumpeter Billie Rogers and vibraphonist Marjorie Hyams, and sought new colors like vibes, clarinet and guitar that Ralph Burns wrote for.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Barnet alumni, Bill Harris and Flip Phillips join the First Herd
segments.summary: Ralph Burns, Chubby Jackson and Frances Wayne came from Charlie Barnet's band; he then found Bill Harris and Flip Phillips.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: The First Herd's impact and its relation to Ellington
segments.summary: The band excited listeners abroad and at home. It took Ellington as its model but tried to capture his feeling rather than copy his music as Barnet did.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Columbia's free hand and the Sinatra-level publicity deal
segments.summary: Columbia, under Manny Sachs, gave him freedom; he asked for the same publicity as Sinatra and Dinah Shore rather than money.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Stravinsky's telegram and the Ebony Concerto premiere at Carnegie Hall
segments.summary: Herman describes receiving a telegram from Stravinsky, who wrote a piece for the band; it was premiered at Carnegie Hall in 1946 and recorded in California.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Columbia people: Goddard Lieberson, John Hammond; Kenton at Capitol
segments.summary: He praises Columbia's Goddard Lieberson and John Hammond's support, comparing it to Capitol's backing of Stan Kenton.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Rehearsing with Stravinsky at the Paramount Theatre
segments.summary: The band dressed up to rehearse with Stravinsky between shows at the Paramount; he rehearsed in a sweatshirt and towel and was unaware they were doing shows.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Bebop contacts: Dizzy writing, Charlie Parker sitting in, Kansas City tape
segments.summary: Dizzy Gillespie wrote for the band and Charlie Parker sat in often; an afternoon Kansas City concert was taped and later released by bootleg labels.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Bop-influenced sidemen and the Four Brothers sound
segments.summary: Shorty Rogers, Red Rodney, Neal Hefti and Conte Candoli reflected modern sounds, and the Four Brothers sound gave the band something new.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Dave Tough and Don Lamond: the drummers of the Herds
segments.summary: Herman describes Davey Tough's timekeeping and discipline, then Don Lamond, whom he gave a free hand in the Second Herd.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Helping young musicians and not asking their age
segments.summary: He says he can help a player who wants help and never asks a young musician his age.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Chubby Jackson's influence and limits as a musician
segments.summary: Herman calls Chubby Jackson a strong influence and spark plug for the band, but says his lack of continued musical study limited him as music grew complex.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Ralph Burns as Herman's biggest success
segments.summary: Herman calls Ralph Burns his biggest success, with Stan Getz second, and wishes Burns could write new music for the band.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: How Herman and Ralph Burns worked: Herman as editor
segments.summary: Herman suggested only tempo for a tune; Burns brought the arrangement and invited him to remove anything that didn't work, giving Herman confidence as an editor.

segments.chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
segments.title: Burns today and his film music for New York, New York
segments.summary: Burns says he no longer writes jazz; he tried to have the band used for a film but wrote music to sound like the band anyway.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Neal Hefti and Shorty Rogers as writers for the band
segments.summary: Hefti wrote few full arrangements but contributed head ideas and fixes; Shorty Rogers also wrote good things for the band.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Black musicians in the band: Royal, Ammons, Jackson, Pettiford
segments.summary: Wong lists black musicians who played with the band; Herman says there was a lot of coming and going.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Loew's Capitol Theatre demands an all-white band
segments.summary: Near the end of the Second Herd, Loew's demanded an all-white orchestra at its Washington theatre; Herman sent the black players to New York for a week, then NAACP lawyers got involved, and Shelly Manne came in.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Bill Harris as the outstanding soloist
segments.summary: Herman ranks Bill Harris among the best soloists in the band's history, a warm man he communicated with perfectly.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Harris's frustrating path: gas company meter reader to Goodman film
segments.summary: Harris was a meter reader in Philadelphia, was rejected at an audition for his tone, played with Bob Chester and others, and waited to join Herman.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Harris and his trombone section buddies
segments.summary: Harris would demand better trombonists, then relent because they were his friends, and made them play far above themselves.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Harris's practical jokes: dummies in the trombone section
segments.summary: Harris and Red Norvo had life-size dummies, one sat in the trombone section; other pranks including the elevator and stage cleats.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Harris's solo Bijou and his original trombone sound
segments.summary: Herman picks Bijou, written for him by Ralph, as a masterpiece; Harris was widely imitated and sounded unlike Dorsey or Teagarden.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Billy Bauer: inhibited guitarist and small-group gems
segments.summary: Bauer was inhibited and anxious, but full of ideas; he later studied with Tristano and appeared at the 40th anniversary.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Conte Candoli joining young
segments.summary: Conte Candoli played summers as a teenager, then joined after graduating; Pete was already in the band.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Red Norvo: long career and unshakeable time
segments.summary: Herman praises Norvo's longevity, taste and steady time, comparing him to Dave Tough.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Retiring for seven months to be with family
segments.summary: At the end of the First Herd he retired for about seven months for his family, then heard Ernie Royal.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Meeting Charlotte in San Francisco, marriage and daughter
segments.summary: Herman met Charlotte in San Francisco while with Tom Garen, married in September 1936 as the band began, and their daughter was born in 1942.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Hearing Ernie Royal and starting the Second Herd
segments.summary: He heard Ernie Royal in Phil Moore's group on Sunset Boulevard, decided to form a band, and Ralph Burns and Jimmy Giuffre helped.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Origins of the Four Brothers saxophone sound
segments.summary: The sound was experimented with by tenors in clubs, and Herman hired Chaloff, Steward and Getz and Zoot; Giuffre wrote the first piece. An uncredited Kenton arranger had done much of the experiment.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Cassette 2 header and fruitcake chatter
segments.summary: The second cassette begins; they chat about a fruitcake and try to recall a trumpet player's name.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Giuffre brings the Four Brothers chart to rehearsal
segments.summary: At the new band's rehearsal studio, Giuffre showed up with the chart; they recorded it on their first Columbia date in California.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Finding Stan Getz
segments.summary: Getz was recommended as an unknown young player; Herman is unsure which band he came from.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Second Herd personnel and recruiting from Washington D.C.
segments.summary: The first band lacked Harris and Chubby but had Sam Marowitz and Earl Swope; many players came from Washington D.C.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Terry Gibbs and the bop feeling of the Second Herd
segments.summary: Terry Gibbs joined in Milwaukee; the Second Herd was based on bop feeling, often leaving the audience wondering.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Ralph Burns's Summer Sequence and Early Autumn for Getz
segments.summary: The first three movements of Summer Sequence were done at the 1946 concert; the fourth, Early Autumn, was written with Getz in mind.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Carlos Gastel brings back original players; the trumpet section
segments.summary: Manager Carlos Gastel insisted on bringing back Harris and Chubby; they try to recall the trumpet section including Bernie Glow and Ernie Royal.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Where 'Herd' came from and the Second Herd's reception
segments.summary: George Simon coined 'Thundering Herd'. The second band met resistance as the band business collapsed at the end of 1946.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Experimenting on the bandstand, not by plan
segments.summary: Herman says his innovations are never planned but mostly done on the bandstand.

segments.chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
segments.title: Ending the Second Herd: work drying up and drugs
segments.summary: Bookings got harder and drugs disrupted the band, so he stopped it.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: 1949 Cuba trip with a small group
segments.summary: After closing the band, Herman took a small group (Manne, Burns, Red Mitchell, Candoli, Milt Jackson and Dave Barbour) to Cuba for a month, booked by Gastel.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Reorganizing with three tenors and baritone; Capitol and MGM
segments.summary: He rebuilt the band with Al Cohn and Zoot; they recorded for Capitol ('Music for Dancing') and then MGM.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Nat Pierce joins the band
segments.summary: Nat Pierce joined in the early 1950s, recommended from the Boston/Berklee contingent, and began writing for the band.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Nat Pierce's role in the 1960s band; emulating yourself
segments.summary: Pierce was a big influence on the 1960s band, hired writers like Bill Holman, and was in and out for 12 to 15 years.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Pierce as road manager and the high point of the 1960s band
segments.summary: Pierce's road manager stint almost became a disaster, but his writing kept the 1960s band focused; Herman sees each period's high point as bounded by its time.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Howie Richmond's Mars label and Mitch Miller's rejection
segments.summary: After a successful 1954 European tour, Howie Richmond started a label when Mitch Miller found the band's Columbia tape unexciting; it lasted a year and a half and was sold to Norman Granz, then MGM.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: The 1950s band's sidemen and which band was the best
segments.summary: He names Fontana, Urso, Perkins, Mettome and Fagerquist, and says each band had something to say.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Network radio shows: Old Gold with Allan Jones and Wildroot Cream Oil
segments.summary: In 1944-45 the band had a short Old Gold show with Allan Jones and then its own weekly Wildroot show that travelled with the band.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: State Department tour of South America in 1958
segments.summary: A three-and-a-half-month tour in which the State Department used the band poorly, sometimes giving one concert a week.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Everest recordings and a planned Ebony Concerto revival in Holland
segments.summary: For Everest the band redid Summer Sequence and Ebony Concerto; Herman hopes to perform Ebony Concerto at a 1980 Stravinsky festival, possibly with Buddy DeFranco.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: South American tour after the Nixon incident and student strikes
segments.summary: The tour opened in Venezuela after the Nixon incident, alongside the New York Philharmonic and other State Department groups; a striking university let them play, but audiences knew little of his music.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Monterey Jazz Festival all-star band
segments.summary: The 1950s were a period of survival; the Monterey band for the Atlantic live album mixed alumni with Sy Zentner and Mel Lewis.

segments.chapter: The 1950s
segments.title: Festival appearances, a Boston Common one-shot, and closing the 1950s
segments.summary: He recalls other festivals and a Boston Common concert tape, says anyone who survived the 1950s should be congratulated, and mentions Jazzland recordings.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Starting the 1960s with a small group
segments.summary: Running out of gas, he took a small group on the road keeping Nat Pierce, Bill Chase and Gordon Brisker as the seed of the 1960s band.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: The Metropole residency that built the 1960s band
segments.summary: The Metropole paid salaries and let them come and go, a cramped place that quickly shaped the band; they place it in 1961-62.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Phillips quartet album leads to the big band album
segments.summary: A successful quartet album for Philips let Herman persuade the label to record the big band, producing Encore in 1963.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Personnel of the Metropole band: Nistico, Chase, Jake Hanna, Southall, Anastas
segments.summary: The band was largely intact: Sal Nistico, Chuck Andrus, Jake Hanna, Nat Pierce, Bill Chase, Henry Southall and baritone saxophonist Tom Anastas.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: European tour and BBC television at the band's peak
segments.summary: The tour was the most successful of its time and the BBC television appearance impressed other musicians.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Nat Pierce's arrangements of Mingus, Silver and Hancock
segments.summary: Pierce dug up pieces by Horace Silver, Mingus and Herbie Hancock (Watermelon Man) and arranged standards, helping audiences understand the band again.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Basin Street West and the live Encore album
segments.summary: On their first Los Angeles visit at Basin Street West the band recorded live, with stars like Nat Cole and Mancini in the audience.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: The post-1969 band: Chick Corea material and Alan Broadbent's writing
segments.summary: From 1969 on the band played composers like Corea, and Alan Broadbent's reworking of Blues in the Night was a triumph.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: College-trained players and Alan Broadbent's recommendation
segments.summary: Music schools, especially in Boston, began supplying technically strong players; Nat Pierce and George Shearing recommended Broadbent.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Bill Chase in Las Vegas and his leaving the band
segments.summary: Chase left the band for Vegas show work and returned or left around 1969-70.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Bill Chase: friendship, racing hobbies and going electric
segments.summary: Herman and Chase shared a love of cars and races, and Herman strongly encouraged Chase's electric group and a new direction.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Jake Hanna as drummer, another peak after Dave Tough
segments.summary: Jake Hanna is seen as a selfless drummer at his peak with the band, though he disliked experiments like jazz waltzes.

segments.chapter: The 1960s band
segments.title: Sal Nistico and handling friction in the band
segments.summary: Nistico was a dynamite tenor who peaked with a rhythm section he claimed to dislike; Herman says a good coach uses psychology to keep players from clashing.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Reading the audience and programming sets on the spot
segments.summary: Herman explains his unpredictable set programming as a sense learned performing since childhood for sensing when an audience is lost.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Deep repertoire, avoiding nostalgia, and a dinner interruption
segments.summary: Herman picks material to suit the audience, using Nat Pierce charts at dance dates; Mrs. Herman interrupts about leftovers.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: The band book and the Woody Herman archives at Houston
segments.summary: He keeps a heavy library of charts, and the University of Houston archives and Berklee hold music that can be reused for students.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Playing high schools and colleges; Kenton's push to teach
segments.summary: Nearly 80 percent of recent dates were in schools and colleges; Stan Kenton persuaded him to do clinics in the 1970s.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Kenton and the unrealized music school idea
segments.summary: Herman tried for years to get Kenton to open a music school staffed by former players, but Kenton always said later.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Better-prepared, school-trained musicians
segments.summary: Young players read well and know harmony; music is more complex than fifteen years ago, thanks to music education.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Feeling and historical awareness in young players
segments.summary: He rejects the idea that young players lack feeling and notes they know stylistic history, such as the current Clifford Brown fascination.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Stage-band alumni communicate with students
segments.summary: Nearly everyone in the band came out of high school stage bands, helping them talk with students at clinics.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Great soloists are not always good clinicians
segments.summary: He only uses players who can also teach; instrument companies overlook that great soloists often can't explain what they do.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: No deficits in the current generation of players
segments.summary: The current young musicians are socially conscious, communicate well and mature on the road, with none of the old silent groups.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Band directors' question: how will my kid earn a living?
segments.summary: The most common question from parents and band directors is about earning a living in music; Herman says if music is the kid's overriding desire they'll do it anyway.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Open forum clinics and the business of music
segments.summary: Clinic sessions are an open forum, including band management and booking, countering the myth of overnight success.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Light My Fire and the crossover backlash
segments.summary: The 1969 Cadet album with Light My Fire was the band's first crossover; it sold well but angered old fans.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: The unchanging hardships of the road
segments.summary: The basic tortures of road life, too little rest, long drives and bad meals, are the same across eras.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: One booking agency controls the bands
segments.summary: The business is harder today because a single booking agency controls bands and there is no competition.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Record companies control the creative process
segments.summary: The financiers dictate albums, hire musicians and have the music written, leaving performers little choice.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Keeping artistic control at his own risk
segments.summary: Herman has mostly done what he wanted, bearing all the responsibility, and finds it harder than ever to reach the audience he knows exists.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Playing Chick Corea's compositions
segments.summary: Recording Corea's music has widened the audience, and he wants more with composers with a broader view without making concessions.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Andy LaVerne's writing and Chuck Mangione as a potential writer
segments.summary: Wong asks about a former band writer; Herman plans to ask Chuck Mangione to write for the band.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: New album, new books and finding a label
segments.summary: The album's new charts are meant to attract a label; he cites a note from Bruce Lundvall that it should be his biggest album.

segments.chapter: Audiences, education and the industry
segments.title: Hearing other big bands: Toshiko Akiyoshi - Lew Tabackin
segments.summary: Herman criticises the Akiyoshi-Tabackin band's very long solos and sketchy writing.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Taking up soprano saxophone after hearing Coltrane at Birdland
segments.summary: Impressed by Coltrane's My Favorite Things at Birdland, he ordered a student-model soprano, having tried one as a boy of about 12.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Recording soprano in 1967 and mutual respect with Coltrane
segments.summary: Herman first recorded soprano on Bill Holman's suite in 1967 and explains Coltrane's respect for him and how he uses soprano for excitement.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: His LeBlanc student-model soprano
segments.summary: He still plays the original LeBlanc student model because the deluxe model had features he couldn't cope with.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: His engraved Selmer alto, stolen and recovered
segments.summary: One of two engraved Selmer altos, once owned by Rudy Vallee, was stolen several times; the State Department returned it after Morocco.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Cassette 3 header
segments.summary: End of cassette 2 and the transcript header for cassette 3.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Buying the engraved alto from Sam Marowitz around 1944-46
segments.summary: Herman bought the alto, found by Sam Marowitz in a New York pawn shop, around 1944-46 when an alto player left, and uses it for ballads.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Johnny Hodges and the Trumbauer influence on his alto sound
segments.summary: He says both he and Hodges were influenced by Frank Trumbauer, and that a feeling for a sound is learned by emulating it.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Criticism of Scott Hamilton for imitating older tenor styles
segments.summary: Herman says Scott Hamilton plays well in the style of Ben Webster and others but that is all he does; he asks that this be passed on.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Imitators of the past and Flip Phillips as a model
segments.summary: Herman likens the imitator to a turntable that never stops and says the young player should hear Flip Phillips' new album and try for new sounds.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Gregory Herbert, a virtuoso who stayed himself
segments.summary: Herman praises Gregory Herbert as a phenomenal saxophonist and flutist who carried tradition while remaining himself.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Recent tenors: Joe Lovano and Gary Keller
segments.summary: He singles out Joe Lovano as a bebop throwback and mentions Gary Keller; several of the group come from Long Island.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Current trumpet section: Glenn Drewes, Jim Powers, Dave Kennedy
segments.summary: He names the current trumpeters Glenn Drewes, Jim Powers, lead player Dave Kennedy, and an alternate; Jay Sollenberger has left.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Everyone plays flugelhorn; Dusko Goykovich
segments.summary: Today every trumpeter plays flugelhorn. Dusko Goykovich was an early such player and wrote I Remember Clifford and Woody's Whistle.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Eastman-trained players widen the band's palette
segments.summary: Classically trained players like Vizzutti and Birch Johnson give the band leeway to attempt many approaches.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Gary Anderson's advice on recording Road Father: start with Fire Dance
segments.summary: Herman recalls Anderson's advice to start the album with the hardest piece, Fire Dance, because if they got past it the rest would follow.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Direct-to-disc recording: no chance to sweeten
segments.summary: Herman says the current album could not have been done direct-to-disc, since it needs overdubbing and sweetening; the performance matters more than how it is recorded.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Chick Corea's Suite for a Hot Band
segments.summary: Corea wrote an 18-20 minute three-movement piece; the first movement should sound like 'Stravinsky meets Sousa'.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: How Corea came to write for the band
segments.summary: After the band's success with La Fiesta and Spain, Herman suggested Corea write a piece, and Corea agreed within days in 1977.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: The Steely Dan material and Victor Feldman's arrangement
segments.summary: A band pianist introduced Steely Dan; Dick LaPalm assigned the arrangements to former writers Broadbent, Stapleton and Victor Feldman.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Tom Scott as co-producer and the lyricon
segments.summary: Tom Scott brought a lyricon for Herman, who handed it back to him; Scott played it on the tracks and co-produced the album.

segments.chapter: Instruments, tenors and the current band
segments.title: Audience reception of the new album on campuses
segments.summary: The album is getting a great reception, especially in colleges where students asked about it for months before.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Most successful European tour: Poland, Hungary, East Germany
segments.summary: Touring Europe since 1954, this tour was the best reception yet, with first visits to Krakow, Warsaw, Budapest and East German towns.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Warsaw Jazz Festival and Polish recordings
segments.summary: The band played the Warsaw festival several times and recorded there from television and radio tapes available only locally.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Summer festival plans and jazz education in Europe
segments.summary: He plans Nice and a seven-hall Dutch festival, and says European jazz education is far behind the US but improving.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Japan, worldwide interest in jazz, and bootlegs
segments.summary: He has toured most of the world; American jazz is widely wanted, and Poland learned it underground during the war.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Which schools to attend: Berklee, North Texas, Eastman
segments.summary: Herman recommends Berklee, North Texas, New England Conservatory or Eastman for brass, and cites Birch Johnson's path from Alabama to Eastman.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: University support for jazz departments versus football
segments.summary: Music departments are poorly supported and can never compete with football and basketball, but progress in the last 15-20 years has been phenomenal.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Hope for a resurgence of big bands from the schools
segments.summary: Herman hopes the best bands in American history come from today's students and that youth will force the record industry and radio to listen.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Big bands, personalities and youth rebelling against the industry
segments.summary: He says big bands didn't need to come back, personalities can be made quickly by whoever controls the industry, and he trusts young people to reject what is dictated.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Public radio and television and their licenses
segments.summary: Herman wants educators to organise to push public TV and radio, saying broadcasters treat public airwaves as personal property.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Money spent on exploitation, not product, and doors closed to young talent
segments.summary: He angrily says the industry spends on promoting punk and ignores abundant young talent, and wants people to act.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Why he distrusts the music educators' convention
segments.summary: Herman says that the jazz educators' organisation has not helped real problems, citing egos he met, and he will not make a speech there.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Educators themselves, not organizations, advanced jazz education
segments.summary: He believes jazz education was built by educators, not groups, and the new generation who played in school stage bands think clearly.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Former band members now teaching in universities
segments.summary: Wong notes alumni are now educators; Herman says most educators have professional experience and the movement can only get stronger.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Herman's modest role and pride in young educators' approval
segments.summary: He says his life has been about entertaining, not organizing, but is proud of young educators' approval.

segments.chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
segments.title: Early jazz education and the GI Bill music schools
segments.summary: Jazz study was once looked down on; early pioneers worked alone, and major music schools grew out of the GI Bill.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: The Sister Fabian-Woody Herman Scholarship Fund in Milwaukee
segments.summary: Herman describes the high school jazz scholarship fund named for his science teacher at St. John's Cathedral, which gives two $2,000 scholarships.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Iowa public television, the 40th anniversary film and Carnegie Hall concert
segments.summary: He praises the Iowa public television crew, the 90-minute 40th anniversary film, and the sold-out Carnegie Hall alumni concert recorded for RCA Victor.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Awards, polls and critics matter less over time
segments.summary: Herman says awards and reviews matter less the longer you live.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Richie Kamuca, appreciated too late
segments.summary: Herman says musicians' estimates improve after death; Charlotte was drawn to Kamuca's haunting playing on the Las Vegas Herd album, and he valued his self-discipline.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Gregory Herbert's discipline and how he joined
segments.summary: Herman calls Herbert the most disciplined young player in years; Wong relays that Richie Cole had heard him in Atlantic City before he joined on tenor.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Frank Tiberi: ten years in the band and his complex tenor playing
segments.summary: Tiberi has been with Herman ten years and brought in Gregory Herbert; Herman admits he often cannot follow Tiberi's complex tenor playing.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Tiberi's doubling on bassoon and other instruments
segments.summary: Tiberi doubles legitimately on instruments like bassoon, giving a classical tone to pieces such as Pavane.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Tiberi's improvisation book and 'Professor Corey'
segments.summary: Tiberi is writing a book on improvisation; Herman jokes he talks like a professor who goes into left field while students adore him.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Tiberi as unofficial mentor and his earlier Philadelphia career
segments.summary: Tiberi helps younger players survive the road; before joining he was a successful Philadelphia studio musician and businessman.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Bill Byrne, road manager and baritone saxophonist
segments.summary: Herman praises Bill Byrne, a Cincinnati Conservatory and Naval Academy Band graduate who handles transportation, payroll and everything for the band; Herman credits him in his troubled period.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Business manager Herbie Dressel
segments.summary: Dressel took over as manager in 1968; he had run a music store and worked in record promotion, was a drummer in early rock and roll groups, and had been a fan since his teens.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: A trying period with a former associate
segments.summary: Herman says a person who started as helpful later had his own problems and Herman was sucked in.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Working for cash flow and years of financial aftermath
segments.summary: It costs Herman more to work than not to, so he works for cash flow and talks daily to lawyers and tax people about problems that began long ago.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Twenty years of tax trouble and his two philosophies
segments.summary: He says he has been in trouble with the tax authorities for 20 years, and cites his upbringing: you weren't put on earth to have a ball, and amassing a fortune isn't important.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: His daughter Inge and grandchildren Tom and Alexandra
segments.summary: His daughter born in 1942 is a bluegrass fiddler in Nashville; grandson Tom plays guitar in a country-pop group, and Alexandra plays clarinet and flute.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Leading as the coach
segments.summary: Asked how much he controls the band, Herman says he is the coach, comparing himself to Woody Hayes and Vince Lombardi.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: Best compliments: the Buffalo bar owner and the McDonald's girl
segments.summary: A Buffalo nightclub owner called him the Vince Lombardi of the bands, and a girl at a McDonald's who recognised him gave the second best compliment.

segments.chapter: Honors, staff, money and family
segments.title: What happens to the band after he is gone
segments.summary: Herman has no long-range plans, no interest in nostalgia efforts, and would only let family carry the name on if it benefited them.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Cassette 4 header and the second session in January 1979
segments.summary: The question of whether it has been worth it trails off; the transcript header for cassette 4, dated January 21, 1979.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Would he do it all again? The music is worth it
segments.summary: Herman says he would do it all over, because of the music, stimulation, people and travel.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: The burden of travel and unprofitable weeks
segments.summary: Long jumps by booking agents strain the band, and bad weeks consume the profits of good ones.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Wartime theatre dates versus one-nighters
segments.summary: In the 1940s wartime limits and week-long theatre engagements, five to seven shows a day, were easier than year-round one-nighters.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Big band experience as a period piece
segments.summary: New big band players aren't realistic; Richie Cole called big band experience a period piece, and Herman says a band working every night beats one that rehearses weekly.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Why few black students join school big bands
segments.summary: Herman sees mostly white kids in high school bands, perhaps from lack of black teachers, and notes Basie and Ellington do not run seminars.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: The Thad Jones - Mel Lewis band as a 'Bed and Board Band'
segments.summary: Herman says the Thad and Mel band was a Monday night band that took engagements just to have a band and fell apart outside New York.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Difficulty recruiting young black players for big bands
segments.summary: Thad Jones had trouble motivating young black players to tour with a big band, and Herman finds fewer black players coming through his own band.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Jim Pugh, a meteoric trombone talent
segments.summary: Pugh first joined as second trombone, but when Bobby Burgess left in the early 1970s he was tried on lead and blossomed, staying over four years.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Eastman brass players: Pugh, Birch Johnson, Vizzutti
segments.summary: Eastman-trained brass players like Pugh, Birch Johnson and trumpeter Al Vizzutti share an approach; Vizzutti was sitting in with the band that night.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Herman's great trombonists and the shortage of trombone players
segments.summary: He lists Harris, Swope, Fontana, Urbie Green, Kai Winding and Frank Rehak, and agrees trombonists are scarce.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Phil Woods on schools producing teachers, and Herman's reply
segments.summary: Wong reads Phil Woods's 1977 quote that jazz is being isolated in academia; Herman finds it amusing but says many exceptional young players will make their own gigs.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: How Sal Nistico came into the band
segments.summary: Herman heard of Nistico through upstate New York, with the Mangione Brothers' Jazz Brothers; Nat Pierce found him and he joined just before the Metropole.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Nistico's gifts and what held him back
segments.summary: Nistico was unmatched for excitement but lacked polish such as intonation; Herman thinks he would have grown with studio experience, though he couldn't be shackled with discipline.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Nistico's European work and place in the Herds
segments.summary: Wong mentions a German big band album with Nistico; both agree he set a model as a swinger, while Herbert's value lay in other facets.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Baritone players: Serge Chaloff, Hipner, Johnson, Smulyan
segments.summary: Frank Hipner was a strange but outstanding player now in Reno; Bruce Johnson is outstanding, and Gary Smulyan from Long Island is a brilliant current player.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Nick Brignola, a stomping baritone saxophonist
segments.summary: Herman calls Brignola, from upstate New York, one of the real giants of baritone in 15 years, with a spirit established players lack.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Gerry Mulligan's new band and the effect of his absence
segments.summary: Mulligan is forming a 12 or 14 piece band playing old Concert Jazz Band music; Herman feels his absence from the scene has not helped his playing.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: How the band recruits: players recommend players
segments.summary: Brignola was in the band a few months in the 1960s. New players are recommended by section members, with an occasional teacher from Berklee or North Texas.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Joe Romano and Bill Perkins join overnight in California
segments.summary: Romano and Bill Perkins joined at the same time in California, among many interesting players of the period.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Bill Byrne handles replacements, uniforms and personal problems
segments.summary: Byrne arranges personnel changes despite geography, supplies ill-fitting uniforms, runs payroll and acts as confessor, while Herman stays out of personal lives.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: Sonny Berman, outstanding at 21
segments.summary: Berman joined at 19 on recommendation of Neal Hefti and others, played greatly at 21 and died that year; a bootleg of the Old Gold radio show reveals more of his playing.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: The First Herd trumpet section: Pete Candoli, Conrad Gozzo
segments.summary: Pete Candoli and Berman were in the section, with lead trumpeter Conrad Gozzo, who had been with Claude Thornhill and in the Navy with Artie Shaw's band.

segments.chapter: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
segments.title: How Conte Candoli joined his brother Pete
segments.summary: Conte visited his brother in summer, was given a chair with Ralph writing parts, and joined permanently when he finished school.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Pete Candoli's Superman stage act
segments.summary: Pete flew down on a wire at the Paramount in a Superman suit before Apple Honey, while the comic Buddy Lester came out in the old baggy suit.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Chubby Jackson the cheerleader and band ribbing, including a fake MGM screen test
segments.summary: Chubby was the ringleader, Sonny Berman copied him, and Ray Linn and others set up a fake MGM screen test for Pete Candoli.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Humor as survival on the road; the East German border incident
segments.summary: Keeping a sense of humor is vital on the road; band members reading Nazi books were held up for hours at the East German border.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Show-business orientation and the dummy playing fourth trombone
segments.summary: Herman encouraged stage antics given his show background, as with Harris's dummy playing fourth trombone at Casino Gardens.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Passaic water fight and a loose operation with rigid standards
segments.summary: On closing night at a new Passaic theatre, a water fight with comic Don Rice led to fire hoses and $2,000 in damages; they never played there again.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Phil Wilson's mad antics in London
segments.summary: Wilson was erratic, and in London staged mock manuscript chaos for an interviewer.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Jake Hanna's gay drummer routine
segments.summary: Hanna always had a topper, and Herman recalls his funny put-on as an auditioning gay drummer.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Travelling by bus after his accident, cars in Europe
segments.summary: Herman has ridden the bus more in two years than in his whole career because of his accident; in Europe he has a car and driver.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Playing for audiences unfamiliar with jazz, such as Africa
segments.summary: He enjoys places he has not been, such as Africa, where communicating musically is a challenge, and finds someone knows jazz almost everywhere.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: The future of music: composition and the American popular song
segments.summary: He won't predict, but says the media are the same faults as for 30 years, and that lasting music needs composition, with American popular songs a vast resource.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Campus interest in arranging and the new album's mission
segments.summary: Schools welcome the arranging material now available; the new album is meant to give dedicated young players more to work with.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Jukebox single, Steely Dan and Mangione follow-ups
segments.summary: A Midwest jukebox operator will put the single on 750 boxes; Steely Dan is interested in writing new material, and Herman asked Mangione.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Planning to buy a lyricon to ease his embouchure problem
segments.summary: Herman plans to buy a lyricon, through Tom Scott's contacts, because electronics avoid his embouchure problem; reactions to its sound on the album have been good.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Few black students in school bands; black bands and education
segments.summary: Most school musicians are white; Herman thinks successful black bands do not share experience, as do some white leaders like Buddy Rich.

segments.chapter: Road humor and looking ahead
segments.title: Kenton, the unbuilt music school and why it's too late
segments.summary: Herman pressed Kenton to open a Southern California music school, but both stayed in the outer world, and it is too late now.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Middle-class Milwaukee neighborhoods of his childhood
segments.summary: Herman describes his family as middle-class movers who lived in five to eight places in north and northeast Milwaukee.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Father's shoe factory career and mother working the line
segments.summary: His father rose over 30 years to an executive in a shoe company, in charge of quality and styling, and his mother worked on a machine there to help the family income.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Extended family, Polish mother, and his parents' deaths
segments.summary: His father was of German extraction, his mother was born in Poland to a large family, a connection that warms Polish audiences; she died years ago and his father about seven or eight years earlier.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: An only child, one cousin, and lifelong Milwaukee friends
segments.summary: Herman was an only child; his one cousin, a history professor, died young, and he stays close to boyhood friends in Milwaukee.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Living above a music store and early odd jobs
segments.summary: The family sometimes lived above stores, including a music store where he tried reeds, a grocery, and he worked at a men's clothing store in high school.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Hollywood films and television work
segments.summary: His first film was What's Cooking? around 1940, followed by wartime musicals including Wintertime, independent features and shorts, and later public television.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Parochial schooling and Sister Fabian
segments.summary: He moved to parochial school by choice because it let him make up work around rehearsals, and mentions Sister Fabian.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Moving to Los Angeles through his wife's family, and upcoming TV shows with Johnny Hartman
segments.summary: Their daughter was born in California where Charlotte's parents lived; the transcript then turns to upcoming Iowa public TV shows, including one with Johnny Hartman.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Buying the Bogart-Bacall house in 1946
segments.summary: Herman bought the Hollywood house from Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall in 1946, furnished, and has lived there 32 years.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: His record collection and bootlegs
segments.summary: He keeps only odds and ends at home; a friend has nearly all his recordings, many from bootleg sources.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Visiting his grandchildren in Nashville
segments.summary: Before Detroit he stopped in Nashville, where his daughter plays bluegrass fiddle as a section musician and grandson Tom has returned to bluegrass.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Recording a country single with Mac Wiseman
segments.summary: Herman recorded My Blue Heaven and If I Could Be With You with bluegrass figure Mac Wiseman, on a friend's small country label.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Singing across styles and the Nashville session method
segments.summary: He has recorded with Bing Crosby, Nat Cole and Dinah Shore, and describes the Nashville rhythm section who work out charts and then he sings to them.

segments.chapter: Early life and home
segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Wong thanks Herman and signs off at Berkeley on January 21, 1979.
